utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, I understand you have a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a brief matter, Your Honour. I just ask permission for Lieutenant-Colonel Raymond Lane. He is a person we are hoping to call as an expert, and I'd ask for permission to have him sit with me in court to assist me in formulating questions for the Defence expert. I believe it's permissible under 90(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know are we done with the preliminary matters? Are we done with preliminary matter or should I call the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have Mr. Martin McCoy today, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may begin, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. McCoy. As you know, my name is Dan Ivetic, and today I'm going be asking you to assist the Trial Chamber with some questions relative to the Defence of Milan Lukic. How do you feel today, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, just one reminder before we get into the actual questioning portion of my discussion with you. Since we are both speaking the same language, and since this all has to get translated and printed up in the transcript correctly, we have to try to kind and pause between my question and your answer to give the interpreters time to catch up with us, and to make sure that we don't both talk over one another. I would ask that you kind of keep an eye on the transcript that's in front of you to assist you in that regard, as will I. Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, for the record, could you please state and spell your full name.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Martin Max McCoy. That's M-a-r-t-i-n, M-a-x, M-c-C-o-y.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, could you just briefly tell us a little bit about yourself? For instance, when and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I was born in the country of the United States, the state of New Mexico, the city of Albuquerque, and that's in the county of Bernalillo, on June 26th, 1973.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, could you tell us where you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I currently reside in the state, in the city of Albuquerque. My physical address is 6308 Mesquite Drive North-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now with regard to your education prior to your employment, could you please give us a brief run-down or summary overview of your educational background.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Starting with high school, I attended a private Catholic high school by the name of St. Pius X High School. Prior to that, I attended Catholic grade school from kindergarten to 8th grade. After high school, I did attend a trade school by the name of TVI. It stands for Technical Vocational Institute. It's like a junior college, per se, and I did take classes in the fire science technology field, and after that I did attend New Mexico State University, where I also took fire science-related classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, first of all, if we could back up for a little bit. With respect to your -- and I'll get back to the post-secondary school and the Technical Vocational Institute that you attended. First of all, where is that institution located?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's located also in Albuquerque, in the city of Albuquerque.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with regard to that particular school, what years did you attend that learning institution?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe it was 1992 to approximately 1994, and it was part-time. I also held a full-time job at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated that you were doing the fire sciences technical field. Could you describe for us some of the specific courses of study that you followed at that institution, the course-work that you undertook.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's quite a large array, from fire tactics, how to actually extinguish fires to fire prevention, how to prevent individuals from starting fires, along with sciences like chemistry and physics, including math and English also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now moving along to the New Mexico State University, I would ask you with respect to that learning institution, what years did you attend?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It would have been the -- I believe it's the fall of 1996 through the fall of 1998, and, again, it's a wide range of classes to include building fire sprinkler systems, fire prevention; also, sciences along with emergency medical training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And with respect to that institution, again, I have to ask you, were you a full-time or part-time student, and if not, what other job were you doing to occupy your time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: During my course of study at New Mexico State University, from 1996 through 1998 I did study part-time at the university because I did hold a full-time position with the Los Cruces Fire Department as a full-time professional fire-fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we'll get to your employment in the various fire departments that you have served in a moment. I'm now trying to finish up with your education. I'd like to -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding that this exhibit that we had scanned in yesterday is not yet made its way into the released e-court. The administrators have not uploaded it, so as to permit me to release it, Your Honours. For the time being, I'd like to have this hard copy of the last page of that exhibit put up on the ELMO just for purposes of allowing us to follow along, and then hopefully the problem will be solved in the interim as I communicate with persons outside of this courtroom to try to get that accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I believe what will be coming up on the ELMO as soon as the -- sir, I believe what's coming up on the ELMO ought to be -- there we go. Could you tell us, what is this document that you provided to me yesterday in the course of our preparations for today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This is my most recent transcript from New Mexico State University --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: -- and it shows all my hours. If I move it up, right there at the bottom, I believe it's a total of 58 hours and a cumulative GPA of 4.0.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to the cumulative GPA, first of all, for those persons in the courtroom who may not be familiar with the American scholastic method of ascertaining performance at the academic level, what is the significance of the grade point average of 4.0 and the grades of A that are listed for the various courses that you took at New Mexico Statute University? In relation to all available grades, what grade is that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's the best grade. It's a letter system along with a number system. A, the letter A, is, of course, the best grade you can get, and it's given the number value of 4; B would be 3; C would be 2; D would be 1; and F, which also stands for failing, equals 0. So on this transcript, you can see all grades were A, which equals a 4.0 average.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to seek your assistance as to what I should do. Should I introduce this exhibit stand-alone and wait for the others to get into e-court? This is electronically part of a larger batch of some 52 or three documents, of which I'll only be going through a handful with the witnesses and the rest would be tendered to the Chamber's -- I don't know which is more convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Introduce it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would introduce this as the next available 1D exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D159, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, did you in fact obtain a degree from this University and if not, why were your studies interrupted?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I did not obtain a degree. I did move from Las Cruces, New Mexico, to Albuquerque to pursue employment with a different fire department at the end of 1998, so I did not finish my schooling at New Mexico State.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I understand that in addition to your formal academic education that we've summarised and gone through now that you have had employment experience and training specific to your profession and line of work. I would, therefore, at this time like to go through some of that, and in order to assist us, I believe I would like to have 1D22-0614 put up on the e-court screen. And sir, what hopefully will be coming up -- no, this one as well. All right. One moment, please. Sir, what I had hoped to bring up was a copy of your curriculum vitae or resume. We'll get that once it comes up, and I'm just going to forge ahead asking you questions about it. Now, first of all, one of things I'd like you to explain for us, where is the first fire department that you worked for that you mentioned at -- that you were working at while attending college?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The first fire department I was employed at was the city of Las Cruces Fire Department, and that's in southern New Mexico. I was one of 12 people selected out of approximately 500 to be hired and start a full-length training academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And with regards to the Las Cruces Fire Department, could you tell us, how many persons did that fire department employ during the time period that you were an employee of the same?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It was approximately 100 to 120 employees. It's been ten years since I've left, so I don't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with regard to the community that you served while a member of that fire department, what kind of community did you serve in terms of the number of residents?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It was approximately 100.000 people lived in the city limits of Las Cruces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for how long? How many years did you serve as a member of that fire department in Los Cruces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Slightly less than three years. It was end of January 1996 when I was hired, and when I left it was beginning of December 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now for those of us that are laymen, that are not fire protection professionals, could you describe for us your basic duties and responsibilities while you were employed at this fire department in Los Cruces, New Mexico.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: My basic normal, everyday duties were to respond to all fire and EMS calls - EMS is an acronym standing for emergency medical service; any type of incident where anyone gets hurt, whether it be a vehicle accident, a fall, a trip; any type of structure fire; wildland fire; vehicle fire; any type of emergency service that was required -- that required the fire department, we would respond, including protecting the aeroport. That was one of my specialties while a member of the Los Cruces Fire Department. I did pursue above and beyond training while I was there to include 96 hours of training at one of the United States' largest aeroports, which would be the Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. They do have a training facility there. They train firemen from all over the country, all over the world because they're a highly-trained aeroport fire department.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just waiting for the translation to catch up with us. Now, you mentioned -- and I want to go into your training a little bit now. You mentioned earlier in your introduction to your employment if this fire department that you attended a 12-week academy. Could you tell us a little bit about that. How many -- first of all, with respect to the training, was it consecutive weeks or spread out? How did that structure?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: For the Los Cruces Fire Academy, it was 12 consecutive weeks, and there -- it consisted of physical activities, physical training every morning, which consisted of calisthenics, jumping jacks, push-ups, sit-ups, along with runs that extended past ten miles. That was just in the early morning hours. And then we would get ready for our day as far as our book-works. We would be presented classes from everything a basic fire-fighter should know from how to extinguish small fires with extinguishers, to using ropes and knots to hoist large equipment up exterior sides of buildings, and then later in the day we would be called upon to do a practical exercise using what we were just taught, the information we were just taught.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And how many hours a day were involved in both the physical and the classroom and application portions of this training academy offered by the fire department?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Physical would be approximately an hour and a half every morning, Monday through Friday, classroom would be approximately four hours in the morning, and the practical application would be approximately four hours every afternoon. And along with these certain blocks of instruction, we would be given written tests that were -- it was required that you pass every test. If you did not pass every test, you would be let go or fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about the instructors for that academy?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The instructors ranged from the rank of fire-fighter, driver, lieutenant, captain, all the way up to the chief of the fire department did instruct classes. They were seasoned veterans ranging anywhere from 5- to 20-plus years of service with the fire department.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you indicated that you had to take tests and if you did not pass all the tests you would be dismissed. Did you, in fact, successfully complete that academy?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is a diploma or certificate from completion of that academy included in the pact that you provide to me, which is the document that we're having difficulty pulling up on e-court at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, with the hope that that document will finally make its way into the system eventually, I would note that at this time that that ought to be page 34 in e-court of that packet, the diploma from the academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to that academy, were there persons who didn't finish successfully?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, everybody did finish successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can you tell me about any other training you received specific to your job while a member of the Los Cruces Fire and Emergency Services?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Restating, I did take the basic fire-fighting class at the Dallas Fort Worth International Airport along with -- I was a CPR instructor. CPR stands for cardiopulmonary, and respiratory. I instructed several hundreds of people while -- with the Los Cruces Fire Department. I also obtained certificates from the organisation, it's called IFSAC, which is International Fire Service Accreditation Congress; and the three certificates I obtained from this organisation are fire-fighter 1, fire-fighter 2, and instructor 1, instructor methodology, which means I am a fire service instructor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you are accredited to instruct firemen in terms of performing their professional duties, and do you so -- have you had an occasion to instruct younger firemen?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and yes, I do. Currently, I'm not assigned to our training academy, but I have taught at the academy regarding certain specialties I have, like aircraft rescue and fire-fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the time period that you spent at Los Cruces Fire Department, did you have occasion to respond to calls involving fires and see first-hand the after-math and effects of fires on buildings and structures?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Often, we responded to house fires, commercial structure fires, church fires, strip-mall fires, so from large fires all the way down to small car fires, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, Mr. McCoy, I believe you testified that you left the Los Cruces Fire and Emergency Service Department in December of 1998. Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I -- after leaving the Los Cruces Fire Department, I went to the Los Alamos Fire Department, which is in north-central New Mexico. This department offered a little bit more pay but also more opportunity for other training along with I lived in Albuquerque, the city of my birth, and commuted to Los Alamos.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I take it that Los Alamos is closer to Albuquerque than Los Cruces was or, Dona Ana county.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Quite a bit closer, approximately 150 miles closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, with respect to the fire department at Los Alamos county when you were serving there, first of all, what size was the fire department in terms of manpower?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Approximately 120 uniformed officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're talking Los Alamos county. With respect to that fire department, what kind of a community did it serve?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The community it served -- that we served and protected was a smaller community than Los Cruces in the numbers of people, residents, but in the quality of hazard or the degree of hazard, it was quite a bit higher. Los Alamos County is the county that surrounds the national laboratory, United States Government Department of Energy's National Laboratory, and we did protect all buildings for the DOE, Department of Energy, at this site. These buildings included plutonium facilities, uranium facilities, along with tritium facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, was there any kind of special theme about your employment there, any kind of special security clearance that you had to apply for and be accredited for in order to operate in securing and investigating fires at these facilities?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Every fire-fighter with the Los Alamos Fire Department is required to obtain a Q clearance. It's equivalent to -- or it is a top-secret clearance, but it's equivalent to a Department of Defence top-secret clearance. They do a thorough background check that goes back 15 years, and basically your background has to be spotless.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to this particular fire department at the Los Alamos County, how long -- what period of time did you serve as a fire-fighter in that department?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I moved from Los Cruces to the Los Alamos Fire Department in December of 1998, and I worked through October of 2001. So again, slightly less than three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to your responsibilities and duties at this fire department, could you briefly give us an overview of that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, very similar to Los Cruces. We were required to respond to all medical emergencies whether they arose from a sick individual, caring for the elderly, or a traumatic injury, like a car accident, or fires, such as structure fires, vehicle fires. This -- the geographic area where Los Alamos is located is very mountainous, and we did have a 50.000-acre wildfire in the summer of 2001 that did threaten and burned a few structures on the national labs along with 250 structures, which are houses, in one night because of this wildfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you render your services in regards to trying to contain that fire and salvage buildings?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We worked shift-work for seven days straight to protect and serve the community. My other duties above the beyond the regular firemen duties were to fix and repair or rebuild - which would be also repair - our self-contained breathing apparatus. I was the only one in the whole department that did this. It's a lot of responsibility. Everybody wears a self-contained breathing apparatus when they enter a structure fire, and it's a lot of responsibility to repair these and send another fireman into a fire with temperatures reaching 5, 600 degrees with a piece of equipment on their back that you repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this one follow-up question as to that before moving on. Did you have to be specially trained in order to be qualified to deal with that self-contained breathing apparatus, and if you could tell us who -- what entity is behind the technical in that apparatus.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I did attend a training school to be able to repair this apparatus, and the brand name is Scott. It's a Scott Air-Pak, S-c-o-t-t, and they're owned by Tyco right now, but the technology, the pressure-reducing technology was created or invented by NASA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for those unfamiliar with NASA, what agency is that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's the aeronautical agency for the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your time-period spent with this fire department, did you have any additional trainings or academies similar to that you had at Los Cruces or in addition to what you had at Los Cruces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It would be in addition. It wasn't an entry-level fire academy. It was a fire-fighter 2 or advanced training academy, and they did observe my time and my experience with a similar fire department; and I was hired as a fire-fighter 2. At the same time, there were fire-fighter 1s who had less training and cadets who had no training hired at the same time as me. When I started the Los Cruces Fire Department, I did have some schooling pertaining to the fire service but no work experience, so I was hired as a cadet - that's with Los Cruces - meaning that I did have a complete, full-length training academy under my belt. I did -- I was able to be hired as a fire-fighter 2 or a fireman with experience for the Los Alamos Fire Department. And again, it was an 11-week academy. It was advanced fire training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to that academy, I want to ask you, can anyone go through that academy, or is there a selection process for the same, and if so, could you tell us what that selection process was and how many persons were selected?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There is a selection process, and have you to interview along with produce resumes and prior training. If you were -- if you didn't have the experience or the training necessary, you wouldn't qualify for the fire-fighter 2. They would put you at a lower level, which would be the fire-fighter 1, or the cadet level with virtually no experience. And out of all the people that applied, there was only five people that were selected for a fire-fighter 2 position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, was there testing involved as part of this academy, and did you, in fact, successfully complete that academy?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. They were testing on a weekly basis along with practical application and written tests. You -- there was a hundred percent success rate. You had to pass every test. If not, you would be terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, once we get the exhibit in e-court, I believe it'll be page 22 that is the certificate of completion for the fire-fighter 2 academy at Los Alamos. Just to verify with the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, was that February of 1999 when you completed that academy?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Ah, we have it up in e-court now. Is this the certificate of completion that we have for the Los Alamos Fire Department Academy, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's signed by the chief, Douglas MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can now have on the screen on one side, 1D22-0614.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Hopefully, that should be your CV. Perfect. And sir, if you could look at this, does this appear to be an up-to-date and complete copy of resume or curriculum vitae listing your various accomplishments and employment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This lacks some of my certificates that I received recently, but it's accurate and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And with the caveat that we'll be going to address some of those more recent certificates a bit later in your background testimony, Your Honours, I would ask to tender 1D22-0614, the document that is tonne left of the screen, as the next available 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, looking at the CV that we now all have access to on the screen, it says that in 2001 you moved to the fire department of the city of Albuquerque, New Mexico, and that is -- is that still where you are currently employed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us with respect to this fire department in Albuquerque, how many fire protection professionals are employed by that department?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There is approximately 700 uniformed fire department employees for the city of Albuquerque.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, to put in perspective for us the employment at this fire department in relation to your previous employment, what kind of community in terms of the number of residents is covered and served within the jurisdiction of the Albuquerque Fire Department?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The city of Albuquerque consists of 500 to 600.000 people. It's a large city. We have over -- I believe it's 22 fire stations, and we have quite a spectrum. We have Haz-Mat teams, he have heavy technical rescue teams. We have swift water rescue. We have a river that runs through town along with many aurials that flow during heavy rains, and we have many areas of specialties within the city and fire department.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me just skip ahead just briefly to try and tie things together here. You've indicated that there are 22 fire stations and approximately 700 persons employed in this fire department. Could you tell us your current position within that fire department, and how many persons in the entire Albuquerque Fire Department system are trained for and do the job that you do?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: My current position with the Albuquerque Fire Department is that of fire/arson investigator. There's seven individuals that do exactly what I do, so that's 1 percent of the fire department is qualified and has the training necessary to investigate fires correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so we can better understand your position within the system, could you tell us, in terms of calls you might be asked to respond to, do they come from a particular section, or do you serve the entire jurisdiction of 600.000 and the entire area covered by the 22 fire stations that make up the Albuquerque Fire Department?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There are times that I'm the only arson investigator on duty to protect this city of 600.000 people. It's a lot of responsibility. There could be three or four fires in one night that I have to investigate. It makes for a long night, but the city has entrusted me with the responsibility of doing the task for solving all the arson crimes in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll get back to your investigative -- arson investigative work in a second. I'd just like to finish up with the other training. Now, when you came to the Albuquerque Fire Department, did you have to go attend an academy similar or in addition to those that you had already attended in your prior posts at the Los Alamos and Las Cruces Fire Departments?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did. It was another lateral academy. Again, this academy was not for an individual without -- or with no fire training. It was an individual who met the requirements of a trained fireman, and they built upon the knowledge that we already had; and it was in approximation about half the length of a normal academy, which I believe this particular academy was nine weeks, and a full-length cadet academy is 18 to 20 weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, with respect to this particular academy, from where were the instructors drawn from, what specialties or experience?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: From the ranks of the fire department. Again, we have driver-operators, driver-engineers that taught some classes, lieutenants and captains that taught others, battalion chiefs and commanders that taught certain classes, but all employees of the fire department. Some of the specialties was Haz-Mat, swift water rescue, high- and low-anger technical rescue, which would include rope rescue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's Haz-Mat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Haz-Mat is Hazardous Materials Training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you successfully complete this academy, and did you obtain a degree or certificate with respect to the same?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I did successfully complete and along with the other academies. Very strict, very stressful. If you fail one test, you're terminated. I'm still employed there, so I did pass all the tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, the bottom of this CV, if we could scroll down to it, I believe has a rendition of some of the certificates that you have achieved. You indicated there are some that are not appearing on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to Exhibit 1D -- pardon me, not exhibit, document 1D22-0615, and I believe it ought to be page 2 of that document, so it should be 0616, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, is this one of the certificates that is not currently reflected on the resume that was submitted, I believe, about a month or two ago?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about the subject matter of this particular -- well, first of all, let's start -- the International Association of Arson Investigators. What kind of an organisation is that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's an international association, obviously, just by the name, but it has certain training, materials, classes, seminars; and it's tailored to the arson investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this in the nature of ongoing training to keep you current with all trends in your profession?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. Again, most of my other certificates are 80 hours, 96 hours, 120 hours. This is a short-tested training programme, but it is continuing education in the arson field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next page, which should be 1D22-0616.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, is this another of the certificates that does not appear on resume relating to your ongoing -- ongoing training in your field?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. This is another short -- it's a 4-hour tested programme, and I am a member of in association, this IAAI, or International Association of Arson Investigators, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For how long -- pardon me for interrupting. For how long have you been a member of that association?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Approximately two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to this particular tested programme, what was the subject matter of the same? If you could describe it for us.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Managing complex fire scenes. This entailed dealing with multi-jurisdictions, multi-agencies, large scenes -- scenes that have -- fire scenes that have resulted in fatalities and how to process them correctly in terms of evidence and autopsies and coroner reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next certificate in line, which would be 1D22-0618, I believe, 7 or 8, actually. 7, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, is this another certificate that is not reflected in the resume that was previously tendered?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is also correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just briefly, is this also on the topic of investigating suspect fires for purposes of determining the cause?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. The title is Investigating Fatal Fires. Fatal fires can be accidental, but they also can be incendiary in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to the specification of your arson/investigative duties in a moment. I'd just like to finish up with your training. Now, the certificates that you have indicated, and you've indicated that some of the academies and courses you took were 80 hours, 100 hours, 40 hours. We have here the packet that you provide to me, which was 1D22-0615 all the way through 1D22-0665, some 53 -- or actually, it looks like it's 50 documents. With respect to that packet of certificates and all the course-work that you undertook while currently employed, how many total hours of training have you undergone with respect to dealing with fires and the aftermaths of fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I would estimate between 2.000 and 3.000 hours, if not more. There's one certificate in this packet that is a certificate for my completion of my police academy, which is 800 hours. That's one certificate by itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can -- my copy's falling apart as we speak. I'd like to -- well, it's in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I think I'm going to do, Your Honours, of course, subject to any objections from the other side, I would tender this packet of certificates, diplomas, et cetera, that is 1D22-0615, up through 1D22-0665, tender that all as one group exhibit rather than individual exhibits to assist the Court, for the Court to have the access to these materials; and I might highlight one or two others individually, but I would seek to introduce just the one group packet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't object per se, but I just would bring to counsel's attention Mr. McCoy's social security number is on the certificate of completion. I'm sure we wouldn't want Mr. McCoy to be the victim of identity theft for having testified here, so perhaps if that one document were sealed or redacted, with you might help Mr. McCoy avoid problems in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with that suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then to just finish up on that before going on to your -- to your arson investigative skills and training, with respect to this packet, at page 13 we have a commendation from a member of United States Congress to you. At page 14, we have a resolution from the New Mexico State Legislator commending your work. At page 15, we have a certificate award from the county of Los Alamos for your work; and at page 16 in e-court, we have a certificate of valour from the United States Department of Energy among your many certificates and commendations. I want to ask you about what is not reflected in there, and that is have you ever had any negative assessments? Have you ever been reprimanded, disciplined, or otherwise sanctioned in the course of your employment and the carrying out of you professional duties?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, sir. In my 13-plus years as a fireman, as a fire-fighter employee, I have never been reprimanded, disciplined, written up in any negative manner. Furthermore, any employment that I've ever had prior to the fire service I've never been written up, reprimanded, or terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, I'd like to turn to your arson investigator -- I should say investigator/suspect arson duties. Could you tell us how and when you obtained the position of fire/arson investigator for the Albuquerque Fire Department as you have mentioned in your testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: In 2006, the spring of 2006 the fire department announced vacancies in the arson and fire investigation division. To qualify for these two positions, you had to be a promoted driver, a driver-engineer. It's a tested position. It's the first position -- first promotion up from fireman, from fire-fighter, and it's a written test that tests your ability to drive a fire truck, drive the ladder truck, and along with knowledge of various fire scenes. And in 2005 I did test and pass the promotional process for driver-engineer; and, therefore, I was able to apply for the position of fire investigator, and there were approximately ten people that applied for this position, and there were two people selected, and, of course, I was one of them, and that was the spring of 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've detailed for us the testing process and the selection process and that you were one of ten applicants who did -- one of ten applicants who applied, one of two who actually succeeded in being appointed to this level. After doing your testing, was there any additional training or academy that you had to successfully complete in order to become employed within the position of fire/arson investigator?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. The first process was a thorough background check, very similar to the background check for my Department of Energy queue clearance. Very thorough. I believe it also went back 15 years, and the reason for that was to be accepted into the state of New Mexico Law Enforcement Training Academy, which is located in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and that consisted of a full-length 21-week police academy. During this academy, I learned everything that a front-line patrolman learns, and I did pass every test again, and upon completion did receive a certificate stating the fact that I am, in fact, a law enforcement officer, which assists me in doing my job as a fire investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify for us, is that the 800-hour course, this being the police academy that you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the course of performing your duties for the Albuquerque Fire Department, are you authorised and powered to carry a firearm and perform arrests and other police functions in addition to your fire prevention and investigative duties?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. I am a full-fledged law enforcement officer. I am commissioned by the city of Las Cruces -- excuse me, the city of Albuquerque police department, the county of Bernalillo sheriff's department to carry a weapon and perform duties as a law enforcement officer. In the city of Albuquerque, arson is a crime, and I have arrested individuals for this crime. I do carry a weapon. I do carry a sidearm. I am required to wear a vest, a bullet-proof -- bullet-resistant vest on a daily basis along with handcuffs to arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are they arrests that you make relating to fires or just general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have arrested I believe three or four individuals relating to fire. Again, fire, arson in the city of Albuquerque is a crime; and I have arrested individuals for that crime, along with recently an individual pulled a weapon out on me, a gun. I drew my weapon out on him, and he was arrested by myself and my superior officer for assault on a peace officer. So I have arrested for other things also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to when you get called out to a suspected scene of a suspicious fire or a suspected arson and you arrive, would you normally arrive while other fire and/or police personnel are still on the scene, and if so, what is your authority as to and over them?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Upon my arrival on any fire scene, I speak to the incident commander, who is the rank of battalion chief or battalion commander with the Albuquerque Fire Department, and he relays any pertinent information to me. Then at that point, I take over the scene. I am in charge of the scene. Anything I need, anything I say goes, whether it's from the police department, from the fire department, or other agencies involved such as utility companies or even Bernalillo County sheriff's department.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And one thing that I skipped was -- I don't know how it is exactly in the fire department, but could you explain to us the situation. Are you currently -- do you currently hold a rank, or what is the situation with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Earlier, I stated I have tested for the rank of driver, which I currently am, driver-operator, driver-engineer. If I was not in the fire investigation office, I would be driving a fire truck. Although I have recently tested for the rank of lieutenant and I did pass the test; I am currently on a waiting list to get promoted to the rank of lieutenant. On my curriculum vitae, there was a section in there where I did upgrade from driver to the rank of lieutenant. We call it acting lieutenant for quite an amount of time. I believe it was three or four months consecutive, so I do have supervisory experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the standard operating practice and procedure of the fire department that you're employed by, could you detail for us the method of work of yourself and fellow fire investigators, that is to say, how is it that your shifts run?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: My -- I do work shift-work, and we work 48 consecutive hours. If my shift starts on a Monday morning at 8.00 a.m., I work all day, all night Monday until 8.00 in the morning Tuesday and continuing all day Tuesday until 8.00 Wednesday morning. I am relieved by another investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to calls to go out and investigate a scene, a location for a suspicious fire, how many personnel from your investigative/arson department would report to a scene? What's the standard procedure?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Standard procedure if nobody is off, if nobody is on holiday would be two -- two individuals, two fully trained arson investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you detail for us in that line of work based upon your experience and training, when the two investigators go on the scene how many -- strike that. What type of determinations do you make? That is to say, how many different classifications or types of causes are there for fires that you've been trained to identify?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Through all my training and experience, there are only four fires, four classifications or fires. The first in no particular order would be incendiary, which is with ill-intent to burn the property of another; accidental, which would include all accidental fires, malfunctions of electrical equipment, mechanical equipment, candles. Candles are a big reason for accidental fires, along with natural or God-created fires, which would be lightening. It's just a classification. And the last would be undetermined.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yourself and your colleagues in the department that do this type-work, search -- the six other individuals that do this kind of work, do you operate under a set of guidelines or rules when you respond to calls and investigate suspicious fires?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The Albuquerque Fire Department has its own specific guidelines relating to the fire investigative field, along with -- we use a guidebook called, it's the National Fire Protection Association, NFP 8921, and it's a guide. We refer to it as a guide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to this publication, NFP 8921, I believe you showed me a copy if it yesterday while we were preparing, is this a -- is this a guide that is distributed within your industry beyond Albuquerque; that is to say, is it in use in other fire departments, and is it accepted in the profession?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. It's widely accepted throughout our profession. It is my opinion that most municipalities throughout the United States, including federal agencies, use this guide along with -- it's accepted as an international guide also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the report that you did specifically for the incidents that are of interest to this Trial Chamber, which we'll get to in a little bit - I'm waiting to get the number for that to see if that's been released into e-court - but you mentioned that you approached the scene, and I believe your colleague also indicated he approached the scene in a systematic approach. Could you describe for us based upon your knowledge, experience in the field what a systematic approach is to examining a structure that is -- that you are investigating for a suspected fire and/or arson?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: A systematic approach in my opinion is an approach -- also the opinion of the guide, is an approach in a systematic manner that's the exact same every time, so you train yourself not to miss anything, and it's also moving from the least burnt portion of the structure to the most severely destroyed portion of the structure, and it's done in a systematic fashion, always very similar to exactly the same -- as close to the same every time. Every building's different, but it's done in a systematic fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in order to examine a site in a systematic fashion, what would be the first steps or the first -- the first examinations as to that site? For instance, if we take Pionirska, for instance, what did you do when you first approached that site?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: First and foremost, being a law enforcement officer, I make sure the scene is safe. There's no threats to myself or my colleagues. Then, I make or do a 360 of the building, meaning I walk completely around the building so I know exactly what I'm looking at, what wall I'm looking at, what side of the building I'm looking at, and if there are possibly any threats unobstructed portion of the building, and while I'm doing my initial 360 or walk-around, I photograph the structure in this fashion, also, so I have a complete 360 photographed documentation of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see we're still having difficulty with your report. Sir, do you have a copy of your report with you today? Maybe we can short-circuit this somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you can pull that out, sir, and I'd like to have that -- with the assistance of the court usher, have that report put on the ELMO for everyone to follow along.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, Your Honours, we've gone through the history and training and educational and professional experience of Mr. McCoy. At this time, I would tender him as an expert for determining -- for talking about fires and the effects of fire upon structures and materials and investigation of suspected fire sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the Chamber would take the step of making a finding that this person, Mr. McCoy, has expertise, the Prosecution would request an opportunity to ask him some questions so that all the relevant information with respect to whether he should be an expert is before the Chamber. In the States, it's commonly called a voir dire. I know in other systems they may have different names for it, but I think before the Chamber makes that determination, each party should have an opportunity to ask the questions they believe are relevant to that particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's perfectly acceptable, Your Honours, and I believe we've been following that the Prosecution gets the opportunity to voir dire after we finish with the witness. If that's how we're going to proceed with this one, I can move on. I'm at Your Honours' convenience, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have no objection to asking my questions in my cross-examination as long as the Chamber were to reserve its finding as to whether they're going to treat Mr. McCoy as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, have you not already challenged the qualifications of this person as an expert under Rule 94 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We notified the Chamber that we were not accepting his expertise, and given the adversarial nature of these proceedings, before the Chamber would reach a final determination about whether he is an expert, implicit in the right to proceed in that way is to ask questions so the Chamber can have all the relevant information before it. Otherwise, it's no right at all to challenge his expertise. I know the Chamber in its ruling reserved its decision about whether it would accept his report as an expert report, but again, if the Chamber is to designate him as an expert now and permit him to give expert opinions without the Prosecution having any opportunity to draw out important information relevant to that, then the point is moot at the time I'm able to challenge it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to find out exactly what the Chamber's ruling was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it helps, Your Honour, but I think we're about 5, 7 minutes away from a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now, and I'll have that matter clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I have before me the decision of the Chamber of the 4th of March, and in that decision we ordered that a number of persons appear before the Chamber as expert witnesses, and included in that list is Martin McCoy, so the Chamber has already made a determination that this witness is an expert. What we did, however, do is to reserve our decision regarding the admission into evidence of the reports of those persons, and his report is among those in respect of which the decision as to their admission is reserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The only response I would have is that Mr. O'Donnell was also one of the people in that decision. I reviewed it over the break, and we actually went through the formal process in his testimony where he was formally tendered as an expert. I didn't contest it, so I didn't ask for a voir dire at that time. I do recognise Your Honour has accurately read that decision. I guess what happened with O'Donnell and, I guess, my sitting here wondering what was the relevance of the last hour and a half if it wasn't about getting out his qualifications and vetting him and getting to a determination if he was already an expert, if he was already an expert -- and I believe there are some questions. And maybe it's a question of what kind of expertise he has, Your Honour. I fully accept that he is a fine fire-fighter. I fully accept that he did a fine job in photographing evidence at the scene, but the question that I have is whether he's really qualified to express an opinion about origins of a fire that started with an explosive. I was thinking over the break the analogy that I have and would offer to the Court is investigators specialise in different fields and one of those might be a homicide investigator, and they are specially trained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I perfectly understand the point you're making. I perfectly understand it, but are you asking us to reconsider our decision, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If that's what I need to do formally, Your Honour, I would ask that it be reconsidered. And the other point that I want to make, Your Honour -- well, just to finish my point, there is a difference between the homicide investigator and the coroner who makes the determination as to the cause of death. It seems when I look at the two resumes of Mr. McCoy and Mr. Dimas, they have the identical expertise, so is there a difference between their expertise? Why are two seemingly very similar people being called to give expertise? So I believe I'm entitled to an opportunity to explore these issue and make submissions to the Court and whether Mr. McCoy is qualified to give that opinion. Again, I do not challenge that he's a fine fireman, and he's done an excellent job in documenting the evidence he found when he examined the scene at Pionirska. It's just whether he's able to make statements about the origin of certain observations he's made, I would challenge and seek to ask him questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you not make written submissions challenging his expertise prior to our decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, based on the resume and the report that we had, we did make those. We did not have the opportunity to speak with him, or we did not have the 50 certificates, Your Honour -- for example, you know, if I give a very practical thing, last night we received the 50 or so certificates. It only in looking at them this morning that I realised that not one of them is for any kind of explosion-based fire. They're all qualifications but certainly nothing that's related to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I had earlier indicated that you'd have no objection to Mr. Groome asking questions relating to the expertise of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Voir diring as to the applicability of this gentleman's experience and knowledge as I believe was the case with other experts that have come here. Your Honours, we intended to, with our presentation, show this man's experience with fires. He's had first-hand experience with fires from 1996 onwards, and now is in a position where he investigating potential fires; and we believe that does qualify him as someone to render an opinion, and we want to show the Court when he gives an opinion or says something what it is based upon, this years of experience. Working backwards from Mr. Groome's submission now as to why there's two persons, that's the area I'm about to ask him about, why there are two persons. It's actually -- the evidence I will elicit will be in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. We are going to consider the question raised by Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to the Chamber that Mr. Groome has raised an interesting point, and the Chamber would in the interests of justice allow Mr. Groome to pose questions relating to the expertise of this witness. However, it seems to us that that should be done immediately because if a determination is made that he's not an expert witness, then he would not testify in that capacity. He could testify but as an ordinary witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just one thing to add, Your Honour, just from the practical side of things. One, the two-man team, and I think Mr. Ivetic was going to touch on that, is sort of a standard operating procedure, as well. But more importantly, and we do take some exception with the theory that Mr. Groome's trying to say that we're presenting, which is that this is an explosive-based fire, we believe that an explosive went off in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah, we don't need to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we are going to adopt the procedure. Whether you call it a voir dire, I am accustomed to that, I think in the civil law they don't have that system; but in any event, I will allow Mr. Groome now to raise questions, and we make a determination about his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can and just with leave of the Court ask -- I have a series of six questions that relate to the procedure and customs and practice of this particular investigator in the course of his employment that details how many fires he has investigated, et cetera. I believe that will be helpful for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You spent a long time on his expertise, an hour and a half. You have two or three more questions. Okay. Ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. McCoy, in the course and pattern of your employment, how many fires or scenes a year and in total have you had an occasion to be involved in from an investigation standpoint?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Approximately 50 fires a year I respond to. A little more than half, about 30 to 35 fires, I'm the lead investigator. I'm in charge. I'm the one that makes the arrests. I'm the one that takes it to the district attorney's office for prosecution, so approximately 50, a little over 50 fires a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about in total during the time-period that you've been employed in as an investigator/arson investigator?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Since graduating the police academy in December of 2006, I have investigated 60 fires that I was the lead investigator on, that I was in charge, that the city of Las Cruces Fire Department left me responsible for rendering decisions on that case, on those cases, and approximately another 60 that I assisted with photography, with sketches, with peer review and rendering -- assisting the lead investigators, investigators, on rendering decisions for those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I believe you meant Albuquerque, I presume, instead of Las Cruces.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just lastly, you indicated assisting lead investigators and peer review. Could you explain for us, having in mind Mr. Groome's concern, why two persons were required with similar qualifications to go to the site. Could you explain for us the ordinarily accepted process and procedure in your line of work in that professional community as to how to conduct investigations of suspect investigated sites and the use of two investigators.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: First and foremost, it's scene safety. When I'm sifting through debris on the scene, bending over with my back to a door or window, my colleague will watch. Most -- some arson fires are a result of a crime concealment, and the criminal might return if they see we're in the room where he started the fire. So initially, it is -- the teamwork is for scene safety along with two sets of eyes is better than one. He might be looking high, I might be looking low, and then we'll switch, vice versa. And along with peer review on every scene: What do you see? I see this pattern on this wall. What do you see? I don't see that; I see this. And we come to a consensus -- we make our own decisions, and then we come to a consensus at the end to call the fire exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just lastly, that peer review and that consensus, where does it take place? That is, do you leave the site of an investigation without having a consensus based upon peer review and confrontation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, it does happen on scene. We confer with each other and defend our case. I think it's this because of this because using my scientific methodology, I find patterns on this wall, in opposed to what he says, or if he agrees with me he'll -- we'll confer. We will not leave the scene without making an accurate decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Now I guess I pause for whatever Mr. Groome is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Before Mr. Groome begins his own examination, Mr. Ivetic, in the Tribunal's case law, an expert is defined as a person who by virtue of some specialised knowledge, skill, or training can assist the trier of fact to understand or determine an issue in dispute. So two questions for you first: What is the area of specialised knowledge, skill, or training that you say this witness has; and secondly, what is the issue in dispute in relation to which his expertise would assist the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The issue of dispute, Your Honours, goes to the heart of the Prosecution's case as to the Pionirska and Bikavac incidents, as to whether, in fact, the evidence on the site, the physical evidence shows indicia of a probability of fire having occurred on that site or not. The report of this expert and the other colleague that he had doing the peer review with is that at the Pionirska site, there was not a fire inside that room where the witnesses the Prosecution stated that there was a long-burning fire. That's the second wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. You have made that clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The first point, Your Honour, just for the record so we're complete, given this gentleman's experience dealing with fire, his training and experience preventing fires, the causes of fires, and ultimately now his most current experience, investigating buildings that have been suspected to be subject to intentional fires, he is, we believe, qualified to talk about the physical evidence on the scene and determine for us when we see a picture of black wood, for instance, whether that damage to the wood is caused by fire or something else, that is to say as someone who is qualified to determine the causes of damage to a structure and effects of fire; he can help us and assist us having been on the scene whether, in fact, what we see is evidence of a fire or not, and that would be the submission for this expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, before I ask my questions, just related to that point, it's not simply a matter of whether there was a fire in the room because I think Mr. McCoy did find evidence of a fire in the room. It's his conclusion that it was the result of children playing or an individual keeping warm, which is I think the opinion that is really at issue. I don't think it's an issue that something happened in that room of a fire nature, just what was the cause of it? Was it as the witnesses described or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Examination on Qualifications by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. McCoy, again, I want to make clear that I have no qualms with your fine service as a fire-fighter or as a fire investigator who has collected evidence and taken very detailed photographs in this case. It is simply about whether you are qualified to be designated an expert and have the status and the ability to give opinions to the Chamber. Now, in transcript page 18, you said that seven individuals do exactly what you do in the Albuquerque Fire Department. Is Mr. Dimas one of the seven that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: His position right now is investigator, but his role is more of an administrative role.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So does he have essentially the same job as you except he also has some administrative duties in your division?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But your expertise you would consider equivalent to his expertise?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Expertise, yes. He does have more experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Longer time-frame in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you have no military training or experience; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you have no experience doing forensic examination in a combat zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly make a pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have no experience doing forensic examination in a combat zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And from looking at the many certificates that you've tendered to us, you have no explosives training; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you said at transcript 27: "Through all my training and experience, there are only four fires, four classifications of fires." And then you enumerated them as incendiary, accidental, natural, and undetermined; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you never mentioned fires caused by explosions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many different types of explosive devices have you dealt with in your work?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, a handful, maybe five, five different ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if there was a fire scene that was the result of an explosion, would you be the person that would do the evaluation, or would someone else be called in to do that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I would be the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would any other specialist be called in, or would you be considered the investigator -- the senior investigator on that type of inquiry?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: If there was a possibility of a secondary device, which a lot of times there are, when police departments or fire departments are involved, if there is that possibility, then I would call in the -- being the commander, I would call in the person necessary, which in my jurisdiction would be the bomb squad, Albuquerque Police Department Bomb Squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They would have someone with expertise particular to fires caused by explosions.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, with taking care of the secondary device.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the transcript at page 3, you said that you took chemistry courses. Now, looking at your transcript from the university, I see that you completed five classes in college and you withdrew from the sixth class; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That transcript shows that, yes. However, if you go to the top, it starts with 41 credits, I believe, and so it's not just five classes that I've taken in college, but I did withdraw from that chemistry class because I did move like I had mentioned. There's not a grade for that class because I did withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the reason was that you had moved to another area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I didn't fail or drop out. I withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So have you, in fact, had any chemistry -- have you completed any university-level chemistry courses.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Not university level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the chemistry course that you withdrew from, it looks like you withdrew rather early in the semester, in October, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, that's when I moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the semester begins in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: August. All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise that just as there's a difference between a homicide investigator, someone trained to gather evidence at a homicide scene, and a pathologist, someone with expertise to determine a cause of death, there's also a difference between a fire investigator, someone qualified to collect evidence at a fire scene, and someone who has the sufficient expertise to advise a Court the origin of the fire.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I'm trained to determine the origin first and then the cause. If the cause of a fire is an explosive device, then that is part of the incendiary portion. If it was done with ill-intent or accidental, there is such a classification as accidental explosions which are it's a natural gas leak or old munitions from World War II that's found in someone's basement, those without the intent would be considered accidental; and yes, I am qualified to make that cause, that origin and cause determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your special training to determine the cause, the origin of a fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Along with on-the-job training, I have two different courses, two different certificates that were not shown. I do not have them. I could get them for you. One is an 80-hour class. It's a 2-week class that was put on by the United States Department of Homeland Security at the National Fire Academy, which is in Emmetsburg, Maryland. The class was two weeks, I believe it was the last two weeks of May in 2008, and prior to that, I had a one-week class, a 40-hour class there was given in Rio Ranch, which is an adjacent city to the city of Albuquerque regarding origin and cause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long in your work have you been determining the origin, the cause of fires?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was accepted into the arson division the summer of 2006, and I graduated the police academy, which is a prerequisite, in the December of 2008. So the beginning -- the end of -- excuse me. The end of 2006, the beginning of 2007 is when I started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you had any practical experience since that time in determining the cause of a fire that actually took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, sir. As I mentioned earlier, I have over a hundred fires, a hundred fire scenes that I've actually been to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, since 2006?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Since 2006, I have been at over 100 fire scenes and assisted in determining the cause or made the determination myself. I am the lead investigator on over half of those fires I've been on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCoy, again, I don't dispute that given your experience just as a homicide detective after a few years of experience will say, Well, I can see that that was a defensive wound or I can see that that was a gun-shot to the back of the head; but there's a big difference between expressing that opinion to colleagues and actually being recognised in a court. So my question to you is, you see from your CV that you've testified in courts in New Mexico; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you testified, have you testified about the steps that you took when you went to a scene, the collection of any samples, taking pictures of the scene?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the US, it's a rather significant step when a person is designated an expert. It's a rather long inquiry by the Court; and the Court makes a legal determination that you are now an expert, and you can give opinions in the court, and you're treated very differently. Have you ever been qualified as an expert by a court in the United States?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, as to relevance. We operate under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this Tribunal, which asking for anyone with specialised knowledge. It's a different criteria than in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see anything wrong in his asking the questions. We make up our own minds as to whether it has any value.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I can add just for -- to exemplify, Your Honour, is in a criminal case a police officer is allowed to testify --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: -- as a police officer. A fire investigator is allowed to testify as a fire investigator.
