In fact, I could provide the New Mexico case law, I could provide the New Mexico case law where being a police officer is not considered expert, but is still allowed to give testimony based on following of the standard operating procedures of their profession and during the investigation. It would only by in a civil arena where a law investigation -- or excuse me, law enforcement of either capacity would be designated as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed with this. I don't want this procedure to be too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Your Honour. I think I'm at the heart of the matter here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you understand my question? Has a judge in the United States ever said to you, Mr. McCoy, given your training, given your experience -- It is usually someone senior in their field who has a lot of experience. You seem to be at a young stage of your career. Has a judge ever designated you as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Don't let my young appearance fool you, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking, has a judge ever designated you an expert in a court?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, they have not, but on my behalf I have given many depositions with fact-based knowledge, factual knowledge that I have scientifically -- with using a scientific methodology come to the conclusion for a case. These are criminal cases, and in the city of Albuquerque, the fire department, the arson investigation division, we hardly ever go to trial because our cases are rock solid. They plea out I'm going to guess 95 percent of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the scientific methodology that you use to determine the origin of a fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We look at all the facts. We gather data. Then we develop a hypothesis. Then we test the hypothesis during our peer review, and then if it passes the test, then that proceeds on to our conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell me some of the science that's involved in coming to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The science is chemistry-based char patterns, visual signs. We also take samples, and yes, I have been questioned in court about photographs I have taken, evidence I have collected, and why this particular evidence was collected. We are very thorough. We're not a shoddy club that you're suggesting --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: We are professionals. We talk to the judges. We talk to the DAs. We talk to people who ask us questions. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that we are determining here is a very narrow one, and it doesn't have anything to do with your shoddyness or not. Any other questions, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just one question that arises from Mr. McCoy's last statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say you make conclusions based on chemistry-based char samples. It's not you that's doing the chemistry and going into a court and saying, Based upon my analysis of the sample --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So that information is given to you by an expert which you then include in your report or would testify to a Court that you received that report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt Mr. Groome, but he's misstating the evidence. He said char pattern, not samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think, Mr. McCoy, you knew what I meant, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: If I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm the one that determines what samples of charred fire debris are collected because of my experience and my training, okay? I am the one that read the patterns on the wall. It's not you. It's no one else in this courtroom that decides where the fire originated, it's me, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But sir --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I have been given the authority to do this by a mayor of a city of 600.000 people. If he didn't think I was qualified to do that, I wouldn't have a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But sir --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There's seven of us in a city of 600.000 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. Sir, please don't get defensive. If I could ask you a question. It's the same way that a homicide detective may come into this room and say make the determination that this glass may have evidential value and collect it; but it's not the homicide detective who is going to do an analysis if the finger-prints match a particular person. That's a very narrow field of expertise. You do have expertise. You have expertise in identifying what needs to be collected, but, sir, don't you agree with me that you don't have the expertise that you can sit here by yourself and without the assistance of other experts in chemistry, in spectography, and all of the very specialised sciences that are used in an arson investigation, you don't have that expertise that you can sit here by yourself and issue an opinion about what causes a fire, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. Referring to this case, 15, 16 years later, I didn't take any evidence, okay. There was no question about a chemist doing his job on this fire. My job was to determine if there was a large fire of heavy intensity inside the basement of the house on Pionirska Street, and that's what I did. There were no samples taken because any aromatic hydrocarbons or presence of ignitable liquid, the fumes would have evaporated over this time-frame; is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. I think Mr. McCoy has valuable evidence to give this Chamber with respect to his observations and the very precise way that he went around the scene and took pictures; but with respect to his report where it draws the conclusion that children started the fire or that the fire was started by an individual trying to keep warm, I would have to, with all due respect to Mr. McCoy, object to his opinion in that regard being accepted as an expert opinion in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. McCoy, when you say that you collect the -- you collect the char patterns. You identify the char patterns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I determine the origin. Then the origin is where in certain cases where an ignitable liquid was poured, whether gasoline alcohol-type fuels, that's -- I determine the origin. Then I take a sample, and I send it to the lab. That wasn't done in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But when you send it to the lab, what does the lab report conclude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether there was a presence of hydrocarbon, an ignitable liquid, or not, and I -- the percentage -- I can't tell you the percentages of times that I collected items that did test positive or not, and it doesn't matter because we take control samples also. We'll take a control sample from something that didn't burn so they know, this is what a piece of wood like -- a piece of wood in the room tested normal, and this is what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it on the basis of the lab report that the final conclusive determination as to the cause, the origin is made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not. It is a compilation of everything, but on-scene, I make the determination what the cause of the fire was and where the origin of the fire was, and I have for more than 60 fires and assisted with more than 50 above that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber's decision by majority, Judge David dissenting, is that the witness does possess the relevant expertise to provide the Trial Chamber with testimony on the cause, the origin of fires. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I believe we had left off with the report that I hope is still up there because I still do not have it on e-court, Your Honours, so with the assistance of the court usher if we could pull that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the meantime, sir, tell me about your examination of the Pionirska alleged fire site. First of all, there's been discussions about your colleague, Mr. Dimas. Whom did you go to the site with, and whom did you perform your scientific methodological inquiry of the site with?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I proceeded to the site on Pionirska Street with my colleague, Benjamin Dimas along with Stephen O'Donnell and Jenkins, Cliff Jenkins, to investigate this scene. Doing a systematic approach, I did a 360, which is a complete walk-around of the structure on Pionirska Street, photographing all sides, all corners, all angles of the house on Pionirska Street, and then finally, entering the structure from the basement level first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what portion of the structure was the focus of your inquiry as to ascertaining what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The focus of my investigation was on the basement of the house on Pionirska Street, the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And first of all, let me see if I can get the number for -- first of all, let's focus on your report for the moment since we have it in front of us. The report that we have on the ELMO, is this a report that was generated by you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when was it generated in relation to your site visit to the Pionirska and Bikavac locations in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It was after my site visit to the house on Pionirska Street and to the site on Bikavac Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the factual observations as well as the specific conclusions that you reached with respect to both Pionirska and Bikavac are set forth in this report. If you were to be asked those same questions in general today, would your answers by the same, with the caveat that we will go through the specifics and look at some photographs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we've already tendered the report in our Rule 94 bis submission, and Your Honours have reserved ruling until the conclusion of the evidence; so I'll move on to the next part of this, which is to start looking at some of the physical evidence that was seen by this witness in his review. If we can call up 1D22-0603 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, we're seeing the first page of a 4-page document. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's a document I put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the photographs are these photographs that were taken by yourself with respect to the Pionirska Street location.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On the first photograph and with the assistance of the court usher, perhaps we can use the pointing marker or device on the screen, the drawing device, I should say. If you could indicate for us in whatever colour would appear well on this photograph, maybe red, with a red arrow on the top photograph where the room that was the focus of your investigation is located.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This is the doorway into the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let the record reflect that it has been done in red. And if we could -- well, before we save this, there's one other item.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And on the second photograph that we have there, next to the window there is an area of discolouration in the wall. Did you have occasion to observe that, and what were your factual observations and findings with respect to that discolouration that you've now marked in red on that second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This discolouration in this area here is darkened wet because of moisture.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the text next to the photograph states: "No signs of fire or smoke damage above the windows." Are those factual findings and conclusions you made base upon what you saw at the site?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why is that relevant to the ultimate hypotheses or inquiry of whether, in fact, this room was involved in a fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: If this basement room was involved in a fire of any magnitude or any intensity, there would be blackened char marks on the exterior portion of these windows. Just like any structure fire, the windows would -- if there was a large fire, the windows would break and the smoke plume would discolour the area directly above the windows that broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let the record reflect that the witness has marked in blue ink the portions relating to whether he would have expected the find the char discolouration from the smoke plumes. If we can save this photograph before moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps if we can ask a general question while the technical aspects of that request are being handled, sir. You've heard Mr. Groome here talk about the room and talk about what he said was a -- was a fire. Could you describe for us upon your visual examination of the room in question, what were your factual findings and conclusions drawn therefrom as to whether, in fact, that room had been enveloped in a large-intensity fire sufficient for 60 to 70 persons to have perished?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Gathering the scientific data on-scene through visual inspections of all surfaces in this room, there was not a fire of great intensity. There was small debris, small diameter, fire -- remnants of a small fire in one portion of this room with many surfaces untouched by fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Where was this area of the room that was -- that had these remnants of a small fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It would be on the floor on the north side of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Describing for us based upon the layout of the room when one walks into it, where would that be located since I don't believe we've had evidence as to what direction the door faces.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The door is on the south side of the room. Again, it's not true south, but it's close enough to call south. Walking through the door -- through the doorway, crossing the threshold, looking straight -- looking due north, that's the north wall. It would be at the base of that wall. There was small-diameter charred debris.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And based upon your experience --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Alarid, who are the other witnesses for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We do not -- Dr. LaGrange is set for tomorrow morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, and we would conclude with her for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, given your experience and work history, what conclusions can you draw from that small -- I believe you called it a small-diameter charred debris. What type of intensity of fire was this, or what -- was it a long-lasting fire? Was it a fire that would have enveloped the whole room?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, it would not have. There, again, like I said, many surface this is this room that were not touched by flame or heat, and I did select the photos that show that. Along with the threshold at the base of the doorway, along with the door frame and the door, there are other pieces of wood embedded in the concrete that are untouched by heat or smoke. They're not discoloured. They're not wet. They're for all intents and purposes pristine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, with respect to this room, it has concrete or brick elements to it, as well, and some plaster. Could you explain for us the principle of heat transference and what one would expect of wood or other material that was perhaps covered over by plaster in a room that was subject to a sustained high-intensity fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: If this room had been fully involved in fire, smoke and fire, every surface would have been discoloured, would have been charred. Every surface of wood would have been charred. Every surface of concrete would have been discoloured by soot, other by-products of combustion, soot, dark silt, smoke. It would discolour, again, every surface. It would be pressurised and every crack, every crevasse, including stuff covered by thin layers of plaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, these particular photographs that we on the screen, the four pages that you had indicated you had generated, you have provided comments next to each photograph. Are those comments based upon your review and conclusions you and your colleague reached based upon your experience and expertise at the scene of this location?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct. We came to a conclusion, many -- to conclusions at the scene, but this document was done in my office with peer review from my colleague, Ben Dimas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the factual descriptions and the conclusions that you have set forth in this document, do you stand by those? That is to say, if today under oath we were to go through each picture, would your observations and conclusions as set forth in this document be the same here under oath?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Of course. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, we have I believe tendered this as part of our 94 bis package, and that's being reserved for Your Honours' decisions following the witness's testimony. I would like to now move to specific photographs. If we can call up Y020-3398, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, as we wait for that photograph to show up on the monitor in front of you, I believe we'll be seeing one of the windows from the location. I would ask you first to identify, if you can, the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This window is the southern-most window. Walking into the room, it's going be your first window on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can pull up side by side with this Y020-3509.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at these two photographs side by side, in relation to the -- can you place this window on the exterior of the house? Are we looking at the same section?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. This window is this window.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let the record reflect that it's been marked in red ink on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you will note that there are no window-sills or window frames in this window. The assertion, I guess, has been made that the -- that there was a fire and that the wood was either destroyed in the fire or removed by whoever set the fire. Do you see any physical evidence of there having been a fire that involved this window?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, sir. There's no evidence of any kind telling me that there was a fire of great intensity in this room by looking at the window, the window-will, or where the window-will would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, assuming for the moment the argument that there was a - let's assume - wooden window-will, and let's assume there was a fire; what types of physical characteristics would you expect to find in the surrounding concrete and in the embedded wood below that would corroborate such a claim that there was a fire that involved the wooden frame of this window? And if you could perhaps use a different colour pen, if you can highlight for us where those physical characteristics or signs would be, markers of a fire.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: If there was a fire in this particular room, there would be signs along this side of the window along with on top dark discolouration and deep embedded discolouration into the cracks, or if the wood was still there, into the wood itself. Even continuing down, depending on the amount of fuel in the room and the amount of oxygen let into the room, how intense the heat was, any porous object in the room, in a pressurised room will succumb to discolouration from the soot and the silt along with the smoke produced from a large, intense fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've marked in blue that area we believe the fire indicators would have been located, and you've also marked what appears to be a wooden slate. That piece of wood that you've marked base upon your visual inspection of the premises, was that something affixed to or embedded in the wall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This particular piece of wood was embedded in the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So that would be a part of the wall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to wood, once it has been exposed to heat and fire, you've already described for us the chemical reaction, I believe, called charring. Once wood has been thus affected by fire, can it ever revert back to an un-charred state?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No. It's a chemical reaction that cannot be reversed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for this screenshot to be saved and given the next available 1D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can go to Y020-3579, and if alongside we can have Y020-3578. The one on the left is a photograph that was in the booklet that the Prosecution tendered for use with Mr. O'Donnell, and for some reason the Prosecution's print-outs appear to have been altered so that they're darker than the original photographs. That's why I'm calling up the originals rather than using the booklet --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a pretty serious accusation that the Prosecution has altered digital files.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not the Prosecution, the scanning process has altered them. It's apparent to the eyes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, does the photograph on the right depict the same portion of the wall as the photograph on the left based upon your recollection of the visual observation of the site at Pionirska?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you will note the darkened area on the right of both photographs. Is that based upon your knowledge and experience as an investigator of fire scenes, does that darkened area or any portion of this wall provide any indicia of a large -- excuse me, of a sustained exposure to fire and/or the results of fire, such as smoke or soot?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No. Upon visiting the scene, this object was not subjected to fire, was not damaged or destroyed by fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the passage of time, the number of years that elapsed? I mean, is it possible that that evidence might have disappeared over time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible. Evidence of any nature would disappear. In this particular room, there was large portions of wooden floor that were untouched. In the time frame that has elapsed since the supposed fire on June 14th, everything could have been replaced. This wood flooring could have been replaced, but in my opinion this is the original wood floor that was in there, that the amount of wear and damage along with moisture, darkening from the moisture, this portion of wood floor appears to be original or dating back to that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so that there's no question in the future, I've asked Mr. Van Hooydonk to take out the printed digital files, the pictures that have been alleged to have been darkened, they were not scanned. We were provided digital files. We printed them, so I have them and I'd ask the usher to circulate them around the court and the Chamber so that the Chamber can see what was printed from the files provided by Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it's only in the book in the PDF format do they have that darker appearance, so I'm assuming they were scanned to make the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They were not scanned. They were just -- digital files were taken and placed in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Printing, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the -- I guess I need to move to introduce both of these photographs. Your Honours, I guess it would probably be best to introduce them separately to give the best possible vantage point for the Trial Chamber as the next available 1D exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You want to have them admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 1D163 and 1D164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can pull up side by side Y020-3618, Y020-3617.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, while well wait for those, you've told members of the Trial Chamber your observations about the wooden floor-boards. The photographs that are coming up on the screen, are these in fact the floor-boards you were talking about in the bottom room of the Pionirska house where the incident was alleged to have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, this is the portion of the wood floor I was referring to and let it be known the dark areas are because of moisture and possible rotting from the excess moisture in time, not charring.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think this is a critical point. I'd like for you to explain to us, again, using the pointer or drawing tool, if necessary. Could you describe for us what areas you're referring to that are moisture and rot but not charring, and explain for us how you determined at the scene that this darkened wood was not the result of charring.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. This area -- I just did something. These portions of the timber that appear darker were, in fact, soaked with moisture from the ambient air, the floor. Again, these windows were open. There's a window slightly above in this direction. It was wintertime, plenty of moisture, and when wood is subjected to heat or open flame, it chars, and it leaves a pattern known in my line of work as alligatoring; and it looks like the back of an alligator, the hide of an alligator, and this wood does not have the alligatoring appearance. It's smooth. You can zoom in and take a closer look, and it is not charred or was not subjected to heat. It's just moisture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you say what the darkened appearance of the wood would have been due to if not the result of a fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without a hundred percent certainty, in my personal experience when you wet wood over a long period of time, it does become darker.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour? Was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Mr. McCoy, when you entered the room, did you note any sources of external water coming into the room?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Throughout the whole interior of this room, it was wet, moist. Above this room is the first floor, and there's vegetation growing. There's grass, and I'm guessing the roof was not intact and there was moisture on the ceiling of this basement, possibly through cracks in the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's take another approach at this wood. Had this wood been exposed to fire and undergone the chemical reaction of charring or creating charcoal, what would the physical remnants or tests be to test for the presence of charcoal? Is there a way you could easily check and it rule out whether in fact something is charcoal?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: As with most charcoal, it'll leave discolouration, it'll leave marks. If you take a piece of paper or even your finger, it will leave a black mark, and tests of that nature were done on this wood, and no residue, no black charcoal or carbon by-product did come off of the wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, looking at these photographs and taking into account what you just said about what you and your colleague did to determine what had caused this wood to discolour, apart from that one small area where there was a small-diameter fire, would these findings and observations be true for the remaining wood floor that was present in this room when you examined it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No. When there's a high intense -- high-heat intense fire in a small room such as this in a structure like this, there's a phenomenon, it's actually a scientific event that happens. It's called flash-over. The surface of everything that can ignite will, and -- floor to ceiling, wall to wall, and if that type of fire occurred, this wood would have charring or alligatoring on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect not only to this portion of the flooring but the flooring throughout this room, which I believe in one of the reports is actually measured and are said how large it is, was there any evidence of flashover or charring of the floorboards?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, there was no evidence of charring to the floorboards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what does that mean to you, the trained observer, as to whether, in fact, there was a high-intensity fire enveloping this entire room?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There was -- in my opinion, there was not a high-intense fire that created a flashover condition in this room because of the untouched surfaces of the floor timbers along with the wood that's embedded in the concrete below the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to Y020-3526 -- pardon, me. If we could save this -- if we could save this picture. Thank you, Madam Registrar. If we could save the screenshot of these two photographs side by side and admit them as the next 1D exhibit number. And if we can have alongside this Y020-3527.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when that picture comes up, sir, I'll ask you to first identify with respect to the door frame of the door, we see certain dark areas on the wood and on both -- and also the concrete. What did your factual observations at the scene determine as to what was this discolouration and whether, in fact, it was indicia of a fire having been in this room?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: My conclusions from these pictures -- or being on scene, this area along with this area, it's obvious that this is mold, green in colour, green in colour, black in colour, moving over, again, green, green in colour, mold. Again, this is a very wet environment. This particular portion is outside. It's exposed to all the elements, and again, the wood in this area -- actually, the complete door frame is untouched by heat or fire, no discolouration, no charring. It's obvious to me that there was no fire of great intensity on the interior of this building. If there was, you would have patterns of smoke exiting out this area in that nature, billowing smoke, discolouring every surface it contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll ask you the same question I asked you earlier about the passage of time and whether that evidence that you would have associated with a fire might have disappeared.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Evidence of what nature? Are you talking ignitable liquids or the charring of the wood?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the charring, for one, yes. What you would normally expect. I mean, what would you normally have expected to see if there had been a fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. In the upper areas of the doorway, the door frame, and depending on the amount of fuel in the room and the amount of smoke coming out of the room, you're going to have discolouration to the door frame, to the concrete above the door, dark discolouration. You're going to have charring from just the heat on the wood. This wood is in pristine condition. Charring is an irreversible chemical change. You can't un-char a piece of wood. It's destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that the passage of time would not have affected that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Once charred, always charred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If, for the record, we can just reflect that the blue markings were the most recent additions to this photograph indicating where the charring and soot patterns would have been. If we could save the screenshot of these two photographs side by side as the next available 1D exhibit and tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you have spent a long time with this witness largely due to the length of your examination relating to his expertise. That was unduly long. Mr. Groome, how long will you be in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a substantial amount of questions and photographs to show this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I would only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that we might be able to sit for at least the first session this afternoon. There's a courtroom available.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine by us, Your Honours. I was just going to add that the nature of this testimony is very critical because obviously it goes toward the truth-finding of the Court to what happened at Pionirska, so I would be happy to -- with the witness's availability, I would be happy to sit an extra session if that's possible with everyone else. I can't speak for everyone in this courtroom, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll let you know later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could pull up Y020-3539. That's, actually, I think 3639. 3639, and also -- let's see what that pulls up before I go looking at other ... okay, 3649, is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, looking at the photograph on the left, sir, and the discolourations to the wood that are evident there, did you observe this phenomenon to the wood that is exhibited in this photograph, and was this related to any fire damage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, no. This picture is on -- is from the interior of the structure, and smoke or flame billowing out from this doorway would have discoloured the upper if not the entire portion of the door frame. Throughout this whole structure, the basement structure, it was very moist, very damp, and this area --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say this, could you mark it --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: And this area is not discoloured because of heat or smoke. It is discoloured, in my opinion, because of the moisture.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Practically speaking, is it possible for fire to skip and create this kind of pattern on wood, or would it be uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It would be uniform. It would be across a portion -- straight across. It's not going to skip this area if there was an intense fire pushing large amounts of heat and smoke, it would have been a line of demarcation where the hot gases were above and then the cool gases were below, the cooler air. So the line of demarcation is not going to skip an area like this. It'll be closer to a line straight across.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let the record reflect, you've used blue ink to denote the second set of your observations. If we could save a screenshot of that photograph and admit it as the next 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could call up Y020-3591, and perhaps -- pardon me, 3590, Your Honours, first, and then also 3634, Y020-3634.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, we're looking at, I believe, the same window that we started our discussion with; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention -- if I could draw your attention to the left-hand side of the window. Do you see that dark line that seems to be curving down from the top of the wall down below the window?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that one that you've just marked in red. Can you correlate that to the photograph on the right as to where that line terminates on the photograph to the right if, indeed, is visible on the photograph to the right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It starts from this black box and then continues down, and in the picture on the left, the black box is right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, based upon your observations at the site and your experience and expertise, were you able to ascertain what this what appears to be a black box is with lines leading to it in four directions?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This black box is a junction box, electrical junction box, and there were wires I believe here, visible wires, and partially visible in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let the record reflect you've continued making markings in red. Was the box itself made of wood or some other material based upon your visual inspection of the same?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Based upon my inspection, it was not wood. It was tin, possibly. I didn't inspect it thoroughly, but I know for a fact it wasn't wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could save this screenshot of the two photographs and mark it as the next 1D exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to 020 -- pardon me, Y020-3633, if we could just pull that up briefly on the screen, having in mind what we've just seen. And if perhaps we could pull the next one up on the left-hand side and leave the right side as is, pull up Y020-3633 on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the photograph on the left that has now come up, is that the same spot you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Again, this area is where the exposed wire was showing and partially in here, and this is a black box, again, of tin, possibly plastic. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And based upon your observations, you are confident that this is not a burnt timber in the wall pocket in the ground floor room.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct. There should be no timber in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, is this near the first window we looked at in one of the first photographs that had the moisture on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Exactly. That is correct. This is the first window to the left once entering the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have a screenshot saved of that and admitted as the next 1D exhibit number. I'd like to then move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are the rest of the photographs of the same kind? What I'm wondering is whether it's going to be repetitive of the same kind of evidence that, it's not a fire. It's due to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The photographs that Mr. McCoy selected and included as part of his report are selection he has comments and conclusions with respect to the same showing these findings. I'm focussing on specific ones that the Prosecution drew attention to during Mr. O'Donnell's testimony and wherein in Prosecution claimed this was wood and timber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now just before leaving the Pionirska house, I have just one other area to do on Pionirska before briefly going to Bikavac, and I'd like to call up number Y020-3539, and -- well, I'll wait for that to come up before I give the next number. And on the right-hand side, if we can have Y020-3540.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now sir, these are photographs that I believe are included in your report, but they're not of the same resolution of these that are now on the screen. They're a little bit less resolution. You mentioned alligatoring in wood. First of all, the wood that is referenced here, where is it located in reference to the room where the alleged fire is to have taken place?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: On the exterior of the basement room.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How far away is this location from any of the windows or any of the doors of the room, the suspect room?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The closest window or door would be the door to this area, and it's approximately 10 feet. The closest window would be approximately 30 feet around a corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is there any possibility for a fire starting in that room to have caused this damage at this portion of the house given the other empirical evidence that you saw at the scene of the crime -- the scene of the site pursuant to your knowledge and experience?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, with my knowledge and experience, fire would have damaged the door, the threshold, the door jam, the door frame to get to this point, to have this kind of damage on the outside of the room, but skipping the door frame is not conceivable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, with respect to this wood, this wood has been burnt; am I correct, and could you tell us what features in this wood identify that it has been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The feature that I'm outlining here is light alligatoring. You can see the marks, the cracks in both ways, up and down. And again, up here, this is larger diameter alligatoring, charring, and the intensity of this fire was not great enough to char this portion all the way through. Again, you have remnants on the backside that -- of clean wood, and going back a little bit in our conversation, this area up here shows little stalagtites or remnants of moisture seeping from the first floor down to the basement level, and again, this is not in the basement. It's in the exterior of the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now looking at the left photograph for a second, there has been a suggestion made that that little piece of untouched portion of the wood is a furring strip that would have been affixed to the wall to have some kind of wall covering. Did you see any evidence of furring strips inside the room that was the focus of your inquiry, the room where it is alleged that the large, intense fire occurred?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No. There was no signs or remnants of any type of furring strips on the interior of the basement, and this one, if you go on a linear -- it's like this, and there's nails up here. You wouldn't tack to an area where there was not a furring strip.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have -- and if the record could reflect the most latest additions were done in blue ink. If we could have this screenshot saved and admitted as the next 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have to push along.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm planning on another 10, 15 minutes tops, Your Honours. If we can have the last two photographs from Pionirska, Y020-3361 and Y020-3360 up side by side on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I suppose soon, Mr. McCoy, you'll have the photographs on the screen of an item that I think you will quickly recognise as the left picture is included on, I believe, your summary report. And while we're waiting for the right-hand side to come up, what can you tell us about this item that is depicted on the left? Where is this, and what is this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This is a picture of a pipe chase or a chimney that -- I'm in the basement looking up. This is -- could be a chimney vent of some kind, and once I walk in to the basement through the door, take two or three steps to the right up against or adjacent to the right wall, which would be the west wall of the basement. And the reason I took this photograph is because this area across is approximately four to five inches in diameter, and this area here -- the whole area, but obvious, it's clean. Fire, heat, smoke, it takes the path of least resistance, which is usually up and out. I've never seen a fire where the smoke goes straight down. It cannot. There's usually a floor or ground or something. It goes up and out, and with this area in the circle being clean, it leads me to believe, again, there was no large fire or a fire with great intensity in this basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you just tell us again, where exactly is this chimney? Is it in the same -- does it proceed from the same room, the same basement room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the basement walking through the door, now I'm inside approximately two or three steps to the right. The windows are going to be on the left, and this chimney is on the right, and the way I photographed it is looking straight up -- from the basement looking straight up. And as you can see, you can see daylight. It's not obstructed. It's a clear path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What would you have expected to see had there been a fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dark markings, discolouration of a dark colour in nature consistent with soot or smoke-staining, similar to the way I drew outside a window where the fire vents. This is pristine. It's spotless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And this even after 17 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. Again, this material in here is porous. It's cinder. It's block or concrete in nature, and it doesn't have a smooth surface. Smooth surface like glass can be cleaned. Soot can be cleaned off it. Porous, it can't. It embeds itself. It's pressurised. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: But is this then a chimney that has never, ever been used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my estimation -- I don't know what the purpose of this particular area going up. It could have been for wires. It could have been a vent for a restroom, a commode. They use vents that vent up sewer gas, which is hydrogen cyanide, up and out so it doesn't -- so you don't get sick from the smell. If, in fact, that was the case, you wouldn't have discolouration. It could have been in the plans for a wood stove of some kind to be used, and it never was. My conclusions of these photographs is that there was no fire in the basement of great enough intensity to discolour a clear pipe chase, an open-air -- you can see there's daylight. It's not obstructed with any rubbish. It's clear and open to the air on the top level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could have this screenshot saved and admitted as the next 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I can then move on to Bikavac, where I'll be rather brief.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If we could first pull up 1D22-0608.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, sir, I believe this will be the summary of the photographs you selected from the Bikavac location. Do you recall -- could you just give us a brief description of what you saw when you arrived at the suspected Bikavac fire site?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have anything on my screen yet, but once I arrived on scene of the alleged Bikavac fire, there were no -- there was no structure. It was completely gone. There were remnants of a footing, a portion of the foundation, not the actual foundation itself, but the footing, along with a walkway that led up towards the house; but in my line of work we need a structure to be able to tell if there was a fire there or not. We need something to tell us direction or intensity or lack thereof; and, again, on this structure, it was basically a vacant lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I think now on the left-hand side we do have this document 1D22-0608. With respect to this, is it something you recall? Is it something you generated?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. These are the photographs I took when I did go to the Bikavac fire scene, and these, again, show the vacant lot, that there's no building. This photograph right here was an adjacent structure, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let the record reflect the witness has marked at the top -- second photograph from the top with a red X.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that red X, again, indicates a vacant structure, and we did find remnants of a building, and it would have been right here to the -- closer from the building with the X, and again, it wasn't a complete foundation that we did find remnants of, but it was the footing. And the house from my findings would have been adjacent to it and looked similar to that as far as the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir. With respect to the Bikavac location, you have made certain findings in your report and have made certain comments giving factual observations and findings in this summary next to the various photographs. If you were to be asked today under oath to comment on these same matters, would your answers to these items be the same? Would you stand by what is asserted in your report and in this factual commentary on these photographs that is in written form?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, Your Honour, this has already been tendered and subject to the Court's reservation of ruling pursuant to the 94 bis procedure. I would only ask that this particular document be screenshot so that we can have the drawings and have that be admitted for purposes of making reference to the witness's testimony the last two minutes thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D171, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, photograph number 5 in this report by you is of a double door.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could perhaps pull up -- let me see. One moment, please. If we can perhaps pull up picture number Y020-3457 alongside.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, what I'd like to ask you is where was this double door locator situated relative to the empty lot where you said that there was a footing or foundation of a house that was no longer there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It would have been on the opposite side. Again, I'm going to -- I'll mark it -- of this structure. So this structure, this structure, the lot where the Bikavac house should have been, and then this structure. So in a row of houses, it would have been this one, then the house that no longer exists, and then this house, so adjacent to it but on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask for a screenshot of -- well, actually not a screenshot. Well, I guess we have to since he's marked on it. Can I get a screenshot of both these photographs and admitted as the next available 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if I can have Y020-3461 up on the screen, and alongside it, Y020-3462.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCoy, did you and your colleague have occasion to -- first of all, who took these photographs of this door?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the time that the door was photographed, did you and/or your colleague have occasion to perform some measurements of the dimensions of this door?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What ought to be coming up hopefully soon might need to be flipped around so we have it lengthwise, rotated, I should say, rotated 90 degrees, as is true with both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And sir, do these photographs accurately depict the manner in which the measurements were taken of the door in question by your colleague while you were taking photographs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we see -- the door appears to be considerably shorter than -- it doesn't seem to be full height. What were the dimensions of the door, do you recall, if that's on your summary report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This dimension is 5 foot, 4 inches tall. Yes, 5 foot, 4 inches tall, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you're indicating the photograph on the left. With respect to the photograph on the right, what portion of the door are we looking at that is being measured there, and according to the measure there appears to be about 9 inches in width?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is just the opening, the windows opening. It's 9 inches.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd ask for these photographs to also be screenshot and admitted as the next 1D exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, subject to just tendering, again, the three items I believe that we have tendered that the Court has reserved ruling on, the report and the photograph set for Bikavac and the photographs set for Pionirska, subject to those three outstanding matters, I have no further questions in direct examination for this witness, and I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. McCoy. I'm actually going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Sorry, Mr. Groome. I should say that we will sit this afternoon. 1.45. What courtroom? We don't know. You'll be informed. You'll be informed. The witness tomorrow is expect to last how long, Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Only because the witness was objected, to I say it could be longer. Dr. LaGrange, in reality the opinion is very short and very technical, so I mean from most of it would be background and what I reviewed, but the opinion itself is short. I would hope to take an hour in total court time with direct exam, and absent to serious challenge to her qualifications, I think that would be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. McCoy, I want to ask you a lot of questions, I want to show some photographs to you. I want to get -- ask you to recount your observations, and the Chamber has found you to be an expert, so I will be asking you some of your opinions. I think we can expedite this if you try to keep your answers short as possible. I don't mean to unfairly cut you off. Recognise that Mr. Ivetic will have another opportunity to ask you questions if he thinks that there's more that he wishes to bring out from you, but I would ask you to try to keep your answers as short as possible. Now, the first question I want to ask you, at transcript page 53, I'm going to quote what you said, and this had to do in relation to your conclusion about there not being a fire inside the room based upon your examination of the exterior wall. Do you remember that? It was early on in your examination.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the quote is: "If this basement room was involved in a fire of any magnitude or any intensity, there would be blackened char marks on the exterior portion of these windows. Just like any structure fire, the windows would -- if the fire was large, the windows would break, and a smoke plume would discolour the area directly above the windows that broke out." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said something similar at transcript page 58: "Dark discolouration and deep embedded discolouration into the cracks." Then you went on to say a few sentences later: "Any porous object will succumb to discolouration from the soot and silt with smoke produced by a large, intense fire." Have I quoted you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in asking you now is, how significant is your finding, no sign of smoke or soot on the building to your finding that there's no fire inside, no intense fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's very significant. Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I thought that. I mean, it seems like a very significant piece of evidence that you've given us your opinion as there was no fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No large, intense fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No large, intense fire. Okay. I'm going ask that we call the picture Y020-3683. Now, my view is that these monitors don't do justice to the pictures you took. You took very high-resolution photos, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I've asked some prints to be made of the photographs. So in addition to seeing it on the screen, I've asked the usher to put a copy on the ELMO next to you so you can see the original print, and there's an additional copy that I'm going be asked to be put up on the Bench so that each of these -- they're in the order that I will use them. I would ask that they get handed up one at a time. I won't use them all at the same time. But I'm going to ask that that first picture, it's Y020-3863. And while the usher is getting that set up, you said that you did a 360 - I believe was the word you used - of the building. Can I take that to mean that you had not only examined the basement, you examined the entire building; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I examined the basement because that was the room in question. I did not do a thorough examination of the complete structure. I was not directed to. This case is a little different. I was told to investigate a fire in the basement. I was not told --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So can we say that you did -- you did examine the entire building, but you did a more thorough and meticulous examination of the room down -- the lower room?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, showing you a picture, it's Y020-3683, can you tell us where you took this picture? It's on the ELMO next to you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Without seeing the ones prior, I couldn't tell you exactly where this was. It wasn't in the basement. I'll tell you that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It wasn't in the basement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I fell you that it is -- the ground floor, we use different terminology here in Europe, so the ground floor, the one above the basement, it's the ceiling of that going into the floor of the first floor above. Do you know the floor I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you rephrase that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the ceiling in the basement was a concrete slab; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the floor on the ground floor, what you and I in America would call the first floor, is a concrete slab; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this is a two-storey structure above the ground.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Above that cement slab?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So this is in between the ground floor and the floor above it, so the bottom portion of this would be the ceiling of the ground floor --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first floor --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Try not to get too confused here. We would call it the first floor in the US, but let's see if we can use, since we are here in Europe, let's try to use what they say. They would say the ground floor where you would come in at the ground, and it's the floor of the first floor, the top floor in the building. How about we do that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is there any doubt that this is terribly, terribly burnt?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No. No doubt in my mind at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if it was the floor above -- in the top floor, it's reasonable to infer that it was covered in wood. There were other pieces of wood that covered this to make an entire floor.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This is not part of the floor itself. This is a beam that supports the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Right. So this is a rather heavy beam, and it actually looks like it's built into the wall; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It appears to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It looks like it's completely burnt.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's not completely burn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe that's a bit of an exaggeration. Substantially burnt.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Less than half of its total mass is gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we can't see any other wood connected to it, so whatever floor-boards, whatever other wood was used to make the structure of the top floor is gone, presumably burnt; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I will not presume that it was burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What do you think happened to it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Fires are very dynamic. If you have beams such as this, the floor will sit on this, and they'll partially burn away, and then when they lose their stability by resting on one another, they'll fall. They won't completely be consumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, but would you characterise a floor that would leave nothing other than this left, would you characterise that as a large fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: If it all happened at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. You're an expert. You're allowed to assume certain facts. Let's say it happened at once. Was it a large fire that completely decimated the top floor?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, but I cannot say without a shadow of a doubt that it did all happen at once. It could have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You can't say that about the basement either, can you? Nothing you can say about the basement is beyond a shadow of a doubt, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: With a hundred percent certainty, I cannot say that this floor burnt at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this. With respect to the soot that you talk about, if the floor-boards burnt on Monday, the fire went out. If the floor beams burnt on Wednesday, fire went out. If the underlying support structure burnt on Saturday and went out, would we see the soot that you're talking about above it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Depends how much moisture's in the air, how much rain this building has received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we zoom out a little bit? I mean, there are a number of pictures like this. I picked this one for no particular reason. Is there any sign of soot or smoke or any of the phenomena that you've talked about above the substantially burnt timber?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes or no, sir, and if there is, can you point to where you say -- the smoke or soot that you can talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There's some discolouration here, here, slight there, and closer there, assuming this wall was not covered at the time of the fire. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if it were covered at the time of the fire, that would be different. You wouldn't see the smoke and soot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Are you asking me to say what this building looked like prior -- at the time of the fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. Obviously you can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is you said that you drew a very important conclusion about what happened in the basement floor based on the absence of soot and smoke in the windows. You talked about the smoke plume going up.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's no doubt that there was smoke involved with this beam, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, there was smoke production.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where is the smoke plume effect that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. Over time, exposed to the elements, again, this is a very moisture-rich climate. This is outside. It's exposed to the elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So -- let me ask you then. So is it possible that exposed to the elements, the smoke and soot that you've talked about can dissipate over time? Yes or no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. On this particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just in theory. Let's talk about theory first. Yes or no, can it dissipate over time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you think that's why on this picture we do not see any evidence of soot or smoke, picture you took about six weeks ago?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, you're asking me -- I mean, it's all encompassing, all-inclusive; to say this is the way the structure was without any wall coverings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. It seems that we're talking about two possibilities: One, there was no covering on this brick at the time of the fire; and two, there was a finished wall surface on this brick. Okay? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's no other possibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There probably is, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you think of one, please tell me what you think it is and we'll talk about this as well.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Many different variations of what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say many variations, what do you mean? Types of wall covering?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yeah. Wood, paper --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's say for the purposes of our discussion now, it was a flammable material, okay?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's take the first instance. There's nothing on this wall. Let's say it was a partially built house or the people didn't finish the walls, okay? Why is there no smoke or soot of the type you've described above this obviously burnt beam?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There is, in certain areas, and if --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you point to me -- you said it would happen directly over the window. So I imagine that if there's going to be smoke or soot here, it should be directly over the source of the smoke.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. There's -- when there's a fire, it's pressurised, and if it's an interior fire, the smoke is going to escape through the least resistant area, being window openings and door openings. So you have dark areas concentrated above these openings, okay? I cannot tell you -- okay, we're saying that this was the floor. If the fire started in the roof of the structure, the apex, and that burnt off, and then this burnt, this floor area burnt, it wouldn't be pressurised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, then. Doesn't it violate the number one principle of fire investigation, fires start down low, and as they burn, they move upward and outward? Fires usually don't start in the roof and work their way down to the basement, do they?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay, you can't say usually. There's so many variations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's say --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've got to let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a phenomenon known as drop-down, okay? Something on fire up high drops down. You're basically saying that there's no attic fires ever, and that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not saying that, sir. What I'm saying is that -- I'm asking you to explain a very simple question. Why is there no smoke or soot directly above what is an obviously substantially burnt beam that's built into the wall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Many variations. Many possibilities. If, in fact, the roof burnt and developed down, the phenomenon called drop-down, something on fire with gravity falls, drops, starts something lower, like this floor, on fire, there's no build-up of pressure to embed itself in the mortar, in the brick, and these bricks are fairly smooth in nature --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's talk about that for a minute. They're actually pretty wide concrete mortar joints between the bricks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the material, as you can see, it's clay. It's a clay brick. I mean, you were there; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the material that they're made of is very similar to what flower pots are made of in the US, is it not? The clay material?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not a flower pot expert or a brick expert. I don't know what material they're made of. They look similar in colour. They're --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting but sometimes we have a problem in B/C/S translation because the speakers are going so fast --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll have to ask both Mr. Groome and witness to observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, likewise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your mike is on, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, are you saying -- I mean, these tiles aren't glazed tiles. There are such a thing as clay tiles that are glazed and have a glass-like surface. These tiles were not glazed, were they?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
