utterances.text: Now, you talk about the reasons why this may not have the smoke effect that you've talked about, is because there may have been a drop-down fire and there was no pressure; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, the portion on the back exterior of the wall where you said you would expect to find the smoke effect, that's an exterior surface. There's nothing to pressure that smoke or to hold it against that wall, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct. Intensity of heat at -- we're talking hundreds, 500-plus degrees in temperature, possibly even reaching a thousand degrees in temperature at that window. The temperature above here is not of such an intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How do you know that? Aren't you speculating now?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. There's BTUs, British thermal units that are measured inside structure fires. It's contained, and the pressure is finally built up enough to release, release the heat through a window. There's nothing keeping in heat or pressure in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, we've -- most of us have the experience of being near a smokey fire or seeing soot, from perhaps a fireplace, collect on the mantelpiece or smoke from a barbecue staining something in our yards. Very often, it can be simply wiped off with a damp cloth; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Possibly in some cases. I do have a fireplace in one of my rental houses, and I lived there for five years, and I cannot get the stain off the brick.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to hear that, but do you allow for the possibility that the weather, 17 years of snow, of rain, of wind could have removed soot from the outside of this building?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Possibly outside, but inside there's pristine -- I mean, it's not inconceivable. I don't know what the annual snowfall is in Visegrad or rainfall, for that matter. I don't know the torrential rains or winds. I cannot comment on the weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you're going to draw such a significant conclusion about the outside of the structure, wouldn't that be something that you'd want to consider? Does it rain one day a year, or does it rain every day of the year?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: In my opinion, there should be -- with an intense fire in the basement, there should be black demarcations above the windows, and for that matter, even more so inside, which there's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me move to a different area now. At transcript 29, you made the comment that the first step that you do when you go to a fire scene is to determine that there are no threats to myself or my colleagues. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So even if there was a very important fire for whatever reason, because of who died in it or what property was in it, would that still be the first step that you would take, to determine whether you and your colleague can safely do your work?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. In peace-time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So is it different than if there's an armed conflict in the area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I can't say. I've never been expose to that type of threat. In peace-time, what I do on my day-to-day job, what I do is I make sure I'm safe, I make sure my partner's safe, and we do the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me just ask the questions, and again you'll have an opportunity to flesh them out with Mr. Ivetic. So in peace-time, no matter how significant the fire may be to the general public or to whomever, still, the number one thing that has to be done is you have to decide whether it's safe for you and your colleagues to go into that building; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the threats that you are going to consider would be the structural integrity of the building, is it going to collapse on you when you're in there doing your job; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps if it's in an area where there's -- the police are having a shoot-out with a gang, you would want to wait until that is resolved before you go in there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: If there's viable patients, viable people that were injured, we would make every effort to make the scene safe and get them out as soon as possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Right. So it's clear, I'm not asking you about the situation where you're trying to save someone's life, that's a different task that you also do. That's a different task than what we're interested in here. What I'm interested in is the task of documenting or collecting evidence at the fire scene. Would you do that in the middle of a shoot-out between police and gang members?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, but it should be done as soon as possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Granted.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: -- afterward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say in your report on page 1, paragraph 2: "Photography of a fire scene is best done during or as soon as possible after a fire to record the scene in an undisturbed condition." Can you explain why that is? What types of information could be lost if the fire investigator is not there as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: If a fire investigator arrives while the fire is still in progress, what we do at that point would be photograph the chain of events as it's happening. If the fire first vents through the ceiling through the roof on the north side, then progresses to the south side, it will heed us -- it will lead us --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Excuse me. My question was simply, what types of information can be lost? Please don't digress into long discussions about other matters. Can you tell me, what other types of information are lost if a fire investigator cannot get to the scene within a reasonable period of time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Reasonable period of time meaning years?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, could I ask you that, if you want to answer that question first. What would you consider a reasonable period of time in which evidence collection has to be done.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Within hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. If for some reason that cannot be done, so we're talking about, let's say, the next day, what types of evidence is lost?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Within a day, possibly the samples -- if you were to take samples of hydrocarbons, areas where you think an ignitable liquid was poured to accelerate the fire. Other evidence like laten, finger-prints, comes from your finger-tips, the oil on the surface, and with time, those go away, time meaning hours, maybe even a couple of days. They could start to degrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So within a few days, we run the risk of losing trace evidence of chemicals that may have been used to start the fire as well as finger-prints; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Within days -- right now, nothing comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. If something does come to mind, please just let me know, and I'll ask you the question again. Now, am I right to say that the longer you wait to look at the scene, the less reliable are the conclusions that can be drawn from an examination of the scene?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That's true, but it does not mean that evidence completely disappears.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, and as we see here, even 17 years later, there are, for example, the burnt beam that I first showed you, that's still there.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I don't know how long ago that burnt, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, while we're looking at this beam, if you were to go up and rub your hand on this beam that's been washed by countless rainstorms, had snow and ice sitting on it for months of the years over the past 17 years, are you saying that if I brushed my hand on it, I'd still come off with black soot the same as if I brushed my hand across a recently burnt log?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, on in particular beam, sir, I don't know. I didn't test this beam.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you agree with me, after a certain period of time --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I can get black marks off of this beam.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: By just rubbing your hand, it'll actually still come off on your hands?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I can get black marks off of that beam, whether I have to dig down lower in the deep-seeded char. This is charcoal. It will produce black.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The floor-boards, did you dig down into the floor-boards?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So when you made your conclusion that it wasn't burnt wood, you talked about -- I can look up the quote, but you talk about there was no transfer of material, and what I took that to mean was that in your contacting it with your feet or just touching it with your hands, no soot came off in your hands. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct. Again, there's other clues, such as the alligatoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, We'll talk about the alligatoring in a few minutes, if you don't mind. But it is possible over time particularly with burnt wood that's exposed to the weather, we can rub our hands on it and we won't get any black soot on our hands; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I didn't -- you say this was burnt 17 years ago. I don't know, and I did not test this particular object.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the passage of time affecting the recovery of evidence, there are -- there's also the weather, which we've been talking about. That's also a possibility; correct? The record can only pick up an audible answer.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the passage of time also creates the potential for someone who wants to trick you as a fire investigator to conceal the crime, gives them an opportunity to go back there and remove evidence or attempt to clean it up; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that's another reason why it's important to get there as soon as possible; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it fair to say to you as an investigator, if there's a delay between the time of the fire and the time that the evidence -- there's an attempt to collect evidence there is a delay, you as the investigator must consider whether that delay has had any impact; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you would consider whether there were people who innocently and inadvertently did something to affect the forensic examination? It doesn't have to be with bad intent. Someone could move in and clean up the place; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So a neighbor with no connection to the case might go in and maybe try to clean it up, try to move into the location; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's not inconceivable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you would need to examine that possibility, would you not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, if it was brought to my attention, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you wait for it to be brought to your attention, or would you attempt to -- would you talk to the landlord and say, Look, has anyone been in the apartment since the fire? Talk to the neighbors, Have you seen anyone --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yeah, we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You would, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you would be active to trying to find out whether anyone had done anything to contaminate the scene or change the scene; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would you also need to consider who might have an interest in the destruction of physical evidence, have the perpetrators of the crime returned afterwards and changed the scene in an effort to conceal what had occurred there; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yeah, it's all possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the 111 fire scenes that you investigated, have you ever had a case in which either one of these things happened, either someone innocently impacted the scene or maliciously impacted the scene?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: In the time frame between the fire was extinguished and I got on the scene, or after I left?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess what I'm saying is during the time that the fire occurs and the time that you're there to collect your evidence, have you ever had a case where someone either innocently or maliciously interfered with that scene before you were able to process it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Maliciously, to the best of my recollection, no; innocently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this investigation, when you were asked to go look at this building, did you ask those questions in this case? Did you consider who might have made use of this structure in 17 years or who might have maliciously interfered with it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There was talk with close -- again, I don't speak the language, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There was talk with neighbors, owners of businesses close by, tenants or occupants of structures, and I'm sure if something like that would have been said, the translators would have informed me of that, that somebody supposedly moved in or remodelled or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you went with a translator to the neighbors, and you asked all the neighbors whether they had any information about someone making other use?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Translator, someone that speaks the language, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please tell me what happened. How did you exclude the possibility that someone moved in and made other use of the property?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: If the person that spoke the language heard of anybody altering the property since the fire, I would have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who's the person that spoke the language?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you were dependent on Mr. Ivetic to do what is an important part of your fire investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I'm not fluent in the language, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You didn't record the results of those conversations anywhere in your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the 111 cases that you've examined, what's the longest interval of time that elapsed between the fire and your examination of the scene?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This one case, it was less than a week, four days, I think, approximately four to five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, looking over your report in this case, I don't see any indication that you considered whatsoever the possibility that in the more than 16 years, some perpetrators or some people attempting to help perpetrators may have returned to interfere with the scene. Did you make any efforts or did you give any consideration to the possibility that the perpetrators of this fire may have returned and to try to sanitise it to remove evidence?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It is a possibility if, in fact, there was a fire; but there's certain items still intact in the basement, in the room that lead me to believe there was not a fire of great intensity. So if there was not a fire of great intensity, why would I assume somebody might have gone back to clean up what --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So let me see if I can follow your thought process. You're saying when you go into the scene, if you do not see signs of a fire of great intensity, there's no need to consider that some perpetrator could have come prior to you being there and taken the evidence that there was a fire of great intensity. Is that what you're saying? Is that your thought process?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: My process -- I went to the scene. There's intact, clean wood in the structure that's embedded into the concrete that could not have been replaced. It's not new. It was there at the time they poured the concrete walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So based upon your discovery of a single piece of wood --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's not single, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many pieces of wood did you find that were embedded in the concrete that had no signs of burning.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The entire door frame including the threshold --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: -- and the single piece of wood you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's the door frame entering, and it's the single strip of wood that's underneath the window immediately to your left?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That's pristine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So based upon your discovery of those two pieces of wood those two areas of wood that had no fire damage, you drew the conclusion that perpetrators could not have returned to sanitise that room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Along with other evidence. It's not just those two things. It's the pipe chase that's clean and not discoloured. It's protected. It's -- there's other -- there's no signs of large fire in this room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the pipe chase. You go back and forth between calling it a pipe chase and a chimney. A pipe chase is a gap in a slab floor that allows electrical wiring and plumbing pipes to be passed through the slab to the floor above; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That could be one definition, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What's the other definition, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Give me a dictionary. I'll look it up for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's a dictionary here, but based on your training, what is a pipe chase? The way that you use it.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It transfers pipes from one floor to another, but it's usually all the way up. And this particular hole or whatever you want to call it, it could have used pipes. There could have been wire -- there could have been a chimney. I don't know what they used it for. I wasn't the designer of this structure. I don't know what their intended use for this hole that goes from the ceiling of the basement floor all the way up. I don't know what their intended use was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, how much longer will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Substantially, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Substantially. You would utilise the hour and a half, this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Fully, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Fully. All right. We'll take the break now, and we'll adjourn, in fact, until 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're adjourning to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Back in this courtroom, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does Your Honour wish to say anything about 15 bis before we proceed? Judge David?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. In the absence of Judge David, Judge Van Den Wyngaert and myself sit under Rule 15 bis. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. McCoy, I've gotten a little bit ahead of myself, and I want to return to the picture that's still on the ELMO. When we were talking about that, we talked about two possibilities: One, no wall covering. But we never talked what would happen if there was a finished wall covering, how that would impact the evidence of smoke. Am I right in concluding or suggesting to you that if the wall was covered with a finished wall covering at the time of the fire, and sometime after the fire the wall covering were removed, that you would not expect to see the types of smoke that you -- the phenomenon that you talked about you expect to see outside the windows; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Without saying exactly what kind of wall covering, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: And there is discolouration. I've showed you areas of discolouration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But I guess I got the impression when you were describing the absence of smoke outside the window, I mean, it seemed something quite remarkable. And when I look at this, I don't see the same type of -- it seems minimal. You say you see it -- I would suggest to you that the darker areas are equally consistent with just dark clay in the manufacture of the bricks.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I'm not a brick expert. I don't know if there is such a thing as dark clay, you know, when you're talking about these red clay bricks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, am I right in suggesting to you that if there were a wall covering, depending on what the wall covering is, it might diminish the appearance of smoke and perhaps even eliminate it.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, what wall covering are you talking about? I mean, wallpaper? Particle board? What do they use in this area, in this area of the world?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sure they use a variety of materials as they use in our part of the world. If there is a distinction to be made between the type of wall covering -- I mean, it seems clear that there wasn't wallpaper on this; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There could have been. I cannot say one way or other what --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You think it's possible that someone would have put wallpaper on this rough brick surface?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There would have bin something hopefully affixed to the brick and then -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we just expedite this by saying -- let's divide wall coverings, finished wall coverings into two types: Ones that are flammable and ones that are not flammable, okay? Do you accept that way of moving forward?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there a difference between surfaces that are not flammable and surfaces that are flammable?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So what would be the -- would a non-flammable surface, finished wall covering, diminish or eliminate the presence of smoke?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Non-flammable such as asbestos would diminish the existence of fire by-product.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. If it were, let's say, wood panelling, would that diminish the existence of smoke. If the outside of the panelling were burnt but was still intact when the fire was out, would that diminish the kind of presence of the smoke you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It all depends on the extent of the fire and how much of the panelling was consumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's say the entire panelling had alligatoring and was charred, the surface that's facing the inside space of the room that caught fire.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: And is there an air space behind the panelling, or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If that makes a difference -- you tell me. Let's say there is an air space behind the panelling.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There would be slight evidence of smoke or soot discolouration on the brick.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if there was a small air space behind the panelling, you expect to see some slight soot, but the panelling would protect the sub-straight, the underlying wall from marks of soot and smoke?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again I think you're trying to back me into a corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get a straight answer. You tell me what the variables are. We'll fix some of them. We'll talk about them but --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The variables on this picture, I cannot say because I don't know if the roof burnt first and it was not a pressurised structure fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But I'm asking you in theory, I'm asking you in theory if there's a flammable wood surface inside with a small air space behind it, am I not correct in saying unless that wood surface burnt entirely through, that even if the outside were alligatored, even if the outside were charred, there would be a diminishment, not complete absence, but there would be a diminishment of the amount of soot that made its way into the rough surface of the concrete; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can just go back to -- I was then asking you about the possibility that people might have interfered -- people maliciously may have interfered with this. Did you ever consider that people wanting to conceal what is arguably one of the most serious crimes that occurred during the war, that someone may have want to conceal that fact from the world?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, that thought did cross my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us about what you considered and how you took that into account in your evaluation of the scene.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: My evaluation of the scene is just that. I looked at the scene. I went into the structure after I did my 360. My 360 revealed no --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, let's not repeat because we do want to try to get you moved along and have other witnesses, so based upon your physical examination of the site, you made a determination that people did not maliciously try to interfere with the site.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So did you make a determination that someone did not, or did you make a determination that someone possibly interfered with this site?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: My determination was that it is slightly possible that somebody went in there and cleaned up, tried to clean up, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, let me just stop you there before we get too far afield.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: But with my experience, I know for a fact that there was not a heavy-involved, intense heat fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you keep coming back to that, but I want to try to break down that conclusion and see how you came to it. Just one second, please. You said that it was slightly possible that someone went in and cleaned up the site. What did you see that made you think that it was possible that someone went into the site and attempted to do some cleaning?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, there was pieces of the floor. Whether they had been completed rotted away or somebody came in and removed them, again, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So there are some portions of the floor that had been entirely removed from the building exposing the earth underneath? Is that a fair statement of what you found?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I don't know how they were removed or who removed them, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So you concluded by seeing that -- you could see the dirt floor, that someone had removed whatever material was above that dirt floor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would I be fair to say that approximately a third of the floor behind the door was essentially gone; it was just dirt?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So anything else other than the removal of that portion -- or the fact that that portion of the floor was missing, anything else lead you to believe that there was a possibility that someone could have interfered with this site?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this is different from many investigations that you've done in that by the time you were asked to look at this site, there were already two people on trial for what occurred here; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever ask any questions, what if -- what opportunity if any either of the people on trial for this fire had to get into this site, what access they may have had to this site?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: You're talking after the alleged date?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. After the alleged date, you think that it may have been interfered with, did you ever ask, Well, the two people that are accused for -- of this crime, did they have access to the site at some point after the fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Again, it misstates the evidence. He never said that he thought -- he said there's a slight possibility. There's a difference, and he specifically stated he doesn't know whether the wood rotted away or was taken away. Mr. Groome is trying to put improper recitation of matters that are supposedly of record, and they are not of record. They are wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see much point in the question, quite frankly; but you wish to have the question answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me put it to you in your context. If you were investigating a scene in Albuquerque. A week had elapsed. You believe that the owner of the business may have burnt it for insurance money, and you believe that some evidence has been tampered with. Wouldn't you naturally try to account for whether or not the owner of the business had the ability to go back in and tamper with the scene?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I have -- I had no information that that happened. You're asking me if -- do I think? I said it's a possibility. I never said in fact it did happen. I don't know for a fact that that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, I'm asking you a different question now. I'm asking, did you ever consider whether the two people accused of this crime, did you ever ask Mr. Ivetic or Mr. Alarid or anyone, what, if any, access did either Milan Lukic or Sredoje Lukic have to this site after the 14th of June, 1992? Did you ever ask that question?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, I never did, but it was my assumption that they lived in this city; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You made the assumption, not me.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That this is -- they were in this city, I believe. Again, it's not my -- wasn't my task to assume where they resided, where they occupied, what structures they lived in. It was my task to find out origin and [Overlapping speakers] ... cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, just conscious of the time. But this case is a little bit different in that there are two fire sites, and we heard you testify in direct examination that there was evidence that the Bikavac fire site had been completed removed. All the rubble's gone from the house; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So someone went to Bikavac and removed the house; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What you saw at Bikavac, you saw the footings and you saw the dirt level with the footings; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Not completely level. There was some grade alterations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it have been consistent with someone taking a bulldozer and just levelling the house and loading the material up into a truck and carting it off?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That would be possibly one way to do it if you can get a bulldozer and are a big dump truck in that tight neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's say you could in Bikavac. What's your opinion as to whether you could have gotten a bulldozer into the Pionirska site? It's a very different site, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It misstates the evidence. He just said he doesn't think you can get it in that neighbourhood, in Bikavac. So again, Mr. Groome is reciting improperly the evidence that is of record and is stating it as if the witness has testified to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the record speaks for itself. I fully expect that the Chamber will not use me as evidence but the words of the witness. I ask that I not be continually interrupted when asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have an obligation, if you are stating the evidence to state it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the Pionirska site, what's your opinion as to whether a bulldozer could have gone down where you walked to examine that room?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It could?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you say the Pionirska site is more accessible than the Bikavac site?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's closer to town. There's not structures that would be in the way of a large bulldozer, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Knowing now -- knowing that the Bikavac site clearly had been interfered with, did you give consider -- full consideration to the fact that perhaps the Pionirska site had been interfered with as well?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Can you rephrase that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I mean, it seems that you're asked to look at two sites. One clearly has been carted away completely. There is nothing, absolutely nothing for to you look at. Is the fact that someone has removed that site, does that not put you on notice to give serious consideration to whether someone has interfered with Pionirska Street fire site?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's a thought in my mind, but obviously not to the degree that Bikavac was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you now about the chimney or the pipe chase. Let's see if we can determine whether it's a pipe chase or a chimney. Now, we've talked a bit about a pipe chase. If it were a pipe chase, it would have some openings to the other floors through which pipes could pass; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Possibly, unless it was straight to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, that's not a pipe chase, then. That's a vent, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's either a chimney vent or I think you said a vent for a toilet; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I did not design this structure. I don't know what the intended use was for that. I know that it was clean on the inside. It did not have soot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Well, my question to you is, there are no openings from that cavity into any of the other floors?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask that Y020 -3444 be called up. While it's being called up, a toilet vent, am I not correct in saying that PVC pipe is the most common material used to make a toilet vent?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. Facts not in evidence, and I don't know if they use PVC pipe in Visegrad and 1992, Your Honour. I know what the building code is in Albuquerque, New Mexico; and yes, you use PVC pipe, schedule number 40, to vent your -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the witness can answer if he's able to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a PVC toilet expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I noticed on your --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: -- for Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I noticed on your transcript that you actually got an A in general construction when you studied for your fire department. Now --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe it was building construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Building construction. And in that course, they never talked about venting?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Building construction is the actual structural components of the building, not the services, the electrical -- it's -- it's not a plumbing class. It's not a plumbing class.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, here's the building next door, and here's a pipe running up the exterior. Is that not the type of pipe that's commonly used to vent toilets?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: With all due respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you're able. If you can't say, then please tell me you can't say, and I'll ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: With all due respect, I do not know what this pipe is made of. I don't know what material. It could be a gutter, carry water off the roof. I do not know what that pipe is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask that Y020-3361 be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not tendering that, so there's no need to save it. I'm go to ask that the witness be given a printed copy of it, again, to make sure that you have the most clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your general construction course --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Building course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Building course, Y020-3361, was it required for the fire career that you were pursuing, the building course or the construction course?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. It's related to the fire service. It did --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that being the case -- I mean, I'm sure at some point you studied chimneys and what materials chimneys are made of; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what a chimney block is?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me explain, and you tell me, maybe you know it by a different term.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ordinary house construction is made by blocks very often 4 inches by 6 inches.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Those blocks are not used when building a chimney because there would be so many mortar joints, there would be a risk of CO2, carbon monoxide, escaping into the living area and perhaps killing people; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: CO, just CO is carbon monoxide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Which ever is the bad one.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. That would escape --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, just yes. We have that. So there's a special block designed for chimneys which is a solid concrete block with a hole in the middle that are simply stacked one on top of the other, and that is hoped to give the best seal in a chimney; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I've never used that method. We -- where I live, we use stainless steel or insulated pipe, metal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, on 3361, we can actually look up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Groome. May I just inquire, are we still in closed session, or are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Open session, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. McCoy, we can see all the way up the chimney here. Would you agree with me that while there are horizontal joints visible, there are no vertical joints in this chimney indicating that ordinary blocks were not used to building it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I mean, do you see any vertical joints?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So we know it's a chimney. Now there are two possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I don't know it's a chimney.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So are you aware of any other, from your construction course that you got an A in, are you aware of any other use in a house where you would build with solid concrete blocks from the basement all the way to the roof?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There are many possibilities, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you name a few of them, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I didn't build this house. I don't know the use of this opening. Possibly, there was a satellite dish on the other structure. Maybe it was to run satellite wires.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you think someone bit this heavy amount of block to run wires for a satellite dish?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why they -- this opening existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- if you would, you're allowed to assume things, and I can ask you theoretical questions.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So let me ask you a theoretical question. If this is a chimney, it seems that there are two possibilities: One, according to you, it was never used; or, two, it was used and either rain over 17 years running down the top of that chimney washed away any soot, or someone cleaned it some other way; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's no cap on this chimney?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It does not appear to have a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say -- I think the word you used is "pristine." There are two pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the actual printed photograph be admitted into evidence now. That's Y020-3361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask that you be shown Y020-3360, another picture you took of the same chimney.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we could have the ELMO on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you take this picture?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It doesn't look quite as pristine in this view, does it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Well, again, shadows and stuff. I mean, on this one it looks much worse than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The 3661 looks much worse, you say?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, no, no. From the -- 3360 to my screen, it looks worse. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which looks worse, the computer screen or the printed copy of --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The printed copy, and it does look worse because of the shadows from the one that was just handed --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, shadows usually travel in a straight line depending on what's create the shadow --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation, outside the scope of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm asking him if he can see smoke in the chimney.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: He's asking about shadows and straight lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the bottom of this, it actually looks like there is not smoke or soot at the bottom of this chimney, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It looks slightly discoloured, but if you look at the other picture it's very clean, and not just on the lip but all the way through. As far as you can see on that other picture, it's clean. And there's no -- after years and year or a day of burning wood, using this as a chimney, you're going to have soot creosote build-up, which sometimes it might go away over years; but all the way up and just a small amount of water coming down the opening, it's going to have a linear striations where the water runs down the interior of this chimney that you're calling it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I tender that into evidence, 3360, and with all of these, Your Honour, I'd ask that not only the e-court version, but the hard copy. Again, Mr. McCoy took these pictures at very high resolution, which is lost on the video monitor, these are actual photographic prints of his files.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm at a loss to how we can proceed. We don't have the ability to make such photographic print-outs. The Defence rooms are not blessed with the same resources as the Prosecution. I'd like to tender the same copies of our pictures as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How do we get them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. You had tendered that into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's P274, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And perhaps just to accommodate Mr. Ivetic, at the end of my examination if there are any of the photos that we printed out that he would like to tender, I'd be happy to provide them for him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you see any concrete signs inside the building that indicated to you that someone had changed it since the time of the fire, either innocently or maliciously?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that Y020-3434 be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to look at the photos of the windows in the room. Did you read the statements of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You did not read any statements?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me tell you what some of the witnesses testified with respect to the windows. They testified that there was glass in the window, in fact it was reinforced glass, and that before escaping at least one woman broke it with her hand after hitting it I think five or six times before being able to escape. Now, knowing that or assuming that there was, in fact, glass in this window, am I correct in suggesting to you that there must have been a frame of some sort, that it would be impossible to mount a piece of glass against the bare concrete as we see it here?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That sounds very conceivable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That if there was glass, there would have been a frame of some type.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And frames are usually wood, aluminum, and sometimes plastic, a vinyl material; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The ones that I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you draw just four arrows to indicate the surfaces where you would expect to find the frame of the window, the material that holds the glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Maybe we can have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, you've drawn a box around the inside perimeter in blue. So it would be fair to say that at least the side surface would have been covered with some material on which to affix the glass.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Inside, meaning --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm talking about the narrow side of the inside of the block; correct? Is that what you intended to draw?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yeah, if it was 3-D, it would be -- you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So it's the width of the wall, along the width of the wall; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the window jams are missing; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: They're not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, didn't you consider that to be a concrete indication that something that has changed since the night of the fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I just saw this structure for the first time two months ago. I don't know what it looked like for the last hundred years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You told us that you didn't read the statements before you did your examination. So did you have the misconception that there was no glass in this at any time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There was not a misconception on my part. I don't know what this structure looked like prior to June of 1992 and after. I do not have that capabilities to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But -- I mean, in your experience as a fire investigator, have you ever seen a fire scene where the complete jam of the window is gone?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. Say that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's no indication whatsoever of the window jam. It's not like there's burnt remnant. It's not like there's a piece on the ground. The window jam that was here is completely missing; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: So you're for certain that there was a window in that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you're allowed to assume facts.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, the way it works is I can't testify. So I'm asking you to assume that the witnesses are correct, that they say -- you seem to frown when I say the witnesses are correct. Do you ever -- do you disbelieve what I'm telling you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I can assume that, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So assume that the witnesses are correct that there was a window here, and it was surrounded by a jam.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The fact that it's completely missing, is that not concrete evidence that someone, either innocently or maliciously, did something to this scene?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to show you the other window --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And actually, I would tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P275, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Y0 -- sorry, I call up Y020-3478, and this is the second window in the room. While it's being called up, did you not recall that there were blocks actually mortared into the second window?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I don't believe they were mortared. They were placed. They weren't --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Let's say they weren't mortared. Let's say they were just placed there in that other window. Is that not a concrete indication that after the night of the fire, someone, either innocently or maliciously, changed the room?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. Innocently or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: -- maliciously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just wait for it to come up, and then I'll tender it, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you want me to read the exhibit number again? It's Y020-3478.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to circle the blocks that are in the window.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, again, in this window, the window jams are missing, and there are blocks in the window instead.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. When you say they're missing, I don't know for a fact that they were ever there, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Assuming that they were there at one point, they're missing now.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Assuming that -- yes, they would be missing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I would tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it seems that an important part of your conclusions here have to do with this door into the area, and I quote you at transcript 65 where you say: "Actually, the complete door frame is untouched by heat or fire of great intensity." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is actually a primary basis for your conclusion that the fire damage we see in the portico just outside the room has no connection with anything that could have happened inside the room; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And because I think you say at transcript 71: "Again, with my knowledge and experience, the fire would have damaged the door, the threshold, the door jam, the door frame, to get to this point. To have this kind of damage on the outside of the room, but skipping the door frame is not conceivable." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your conclusion that in addition to whatever children lit fires or whatever people lit fires inside the room to stay warm, there was another fire at a different time in the portico?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you able to characterise the magnitude of that fire based on your examination of the alligatoring?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Being that there's still remnants of the flammables on the wood, the untouched wood, it wasn't -- in my opinion, it wasn't that intense of a fire. If it was, it would have completely destroyed all the remaining wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on page 3 of the report, my question -- well, you talk about the door, so my question to you is, did you consider whether the door and the door frame were the original door frame that were there on the night of the fire, or did you just assume that they were?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I did consider that fact, and we did -- me and my colleague looked at the door thoroughly, along with photographing it thoroughly, and we came to the conclusion that it was there. It was -- it's the original door because of the way it's set into the concrete. If you show some photos, I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe you could just list them for me now. So it was set into the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What else made you think that it was -- or made you believe or conclude that it was the same door?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, through overhearing my colleague speak, the door opens inward, and I believe someone said there was an explosion or it would have pushed the door outward, and the door -- someone said at some point the door went outward, and that's not true. The door --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This door swings inside.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So did you read statements, or did you not read statements?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I said overhearing my colleagues talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So let's take a look at that door, and let's explore that a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I please ask that Y020-3526 be called up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I saw pictures of the mission. You all seemed -- or the trip to the site. It seemed that you were all wearing heavy clothes. Was it cold at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Very.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are we able to call that up? While it's being called up, if -- is the Registrar -- looks like something's happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's 3526, counsel. I don't know if that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's not the picture I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you recall there's a gap to the right of the door, between the door jam and the concrete. Is there not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I think there is at some point along the frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you draw any conclusion from that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we look at Y020-3348.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now -- maybe if we look to the right now, can you see the gap that I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to circle that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that's the gap. Now, look to the left. Now, what we're looking at is that the edge of the door, the door is swung into the room; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the mortice for the lock set, we can see that here, can we not, the hollowed-out portion of the door where the lock is inserted?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you circle that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. The counsel is testifying, and maybe I just don't see what he sees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm talking with a man who got an A in construction, and I can ask a leading question. If he knows, he knows. And he has said yes that he does know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please circle the mortice where the lock set would be.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There is a hole right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that's affixed to the same side of the door as the hinges, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's on the same side as the hinges, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you ever in your life seen a door where the doorknob is on the same side of the door as the hinges are on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. If you show other pictures of this door, there's also one --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Maybe just answer my question. Have you ever seen a door like that, where the lock set is on the same side of the door as the hinges?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: To the -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, is that not unequivocal evidence that this may not be the door?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I don't know if this room was ever tenable. I don't know if they used it as a barn. I don't know what this room was used for. If this is the original door, it could have been a remanufactured original door. I mean, if you go to this area, you know these people are not wealthy. They use old bricks to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let's not make generalisations about the people in the area. They to do their best to stay warm in the cold winter. I tender this, and let's look at some other pictures of the door. Now, when you -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P277.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Two of the witnesses gave evidence that when they were forced into the room, they actually heard the look being turned -- locked behind them.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you overhear that before you went to the scene? Had you heard that, would that have made you more concerned with looking at a door that it's physically impossible to lock because the doorknob and the lock are on the same side as the hinges?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. It's physically possible that this door had a lock on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you never entertained the possibility that this might not be the original door that was there the 14th? You concluded that it was?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I tender that, and I'm going to show you another door. I think this will have the other mark that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P278.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This picture's from the exact same perspective, but in this case the door is closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there a problem with the computer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, now we're looking at the door, the same perspective. The door is closed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, there's a small black or small brown square to the right. Is that the place where you're saying might have been a lock set?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe so. Something in this area, you know, could have made -- could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please circle -- maybe, could you make a more precise circle or draw an arrow to the thing that you think may be evidence that a lock set was on the right side of the door.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I cannot tell with this picture. I see something black, but I don't know what that is. You're leading me to believe that I think that's a lock set.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There's something black and square. I want a better picture. I know there's a better picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you said that there was something on the other side that you believe might be a lock set. Can you point -- can you circle that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that's the point that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, again, there's a better picture. I know I took a better picture than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I was given 450. Maybe during the break we can make arrangements for you to look and you can find what you think is a better picture. But this is the portion of the door that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if the lock set is there, there would have to be another indentation in the door jam for the lock set to fit into; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I would imagine so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And there is none on this door jam, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Is there a better picture? Can you find me a better picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will try to find you a better picture. Let me ask you from your independent recollection as you sit here today, when you examine the door jam, and it seems you examined it quite carefully, did you see any indentation on the door jam where the bolt of the door would fit?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: To the best -- to my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I can't say for certain that there was an indentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, but --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: But I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you don't recall, or your best recollection is there's none?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So let me tender this now, and then I'll show you a couple more pictures.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that you be shown Y020-3543, and I'm going to also ask -- I'm sorry, that's Y020-3543 and Y020-3639.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If both of those could be placed on the screen at the same time. We could remove this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, while this is being brought up, looking into the room, at the top left-hand side of the door, there is a piece of wood. I think you and I would refer to it as a 2 by 4, the rough dimensions of the wood, that is used as a wedge to secure the door jam; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yeah, it looks something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it looks like a temporary thing. It doesn't look like a permanent fixture of the door, does it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I don't know the construction techniques for basements in Visegrad --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's go with what you know. Have you ever seen a permanent finished door have a piece of wood hammered in or jammed in to the side to hold it up?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation, relevance, unless he leads a foundation that this witness has seen doors in Visegrad and Bosnia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen doors with shims in them; when they're finished, they're covered --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This isn't a door shim, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the transcript has recorded you as saying specks league of nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that was speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is not a door shim, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Sir, with all due respect, I would call this a door shim.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask that we have the photo of this. I'm going to ask that it be placed on the ELMO in front of you, Y020-3639, and there's also a copy for the Bench. I'd ask -- it's all there in the order that I had used them. I ask that it be passed up to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we get a copy, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They're your pictures, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I put a little yellow tag to show you the portion of this 2 by 4 or this wedge that I want to address with you. To the lay-eye, it looks charred. It looks like there's white ash on it. It looks burnt. Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object from the standpoint of inconsistent theories. Mr. Groome's, on one hand, postulating that this door was ex post facto and part of a tampering process wherein the door was replaced or otherwise reconstructed, and then on the secondhand arguing the same thing that that same exact door frame that could have been installed after the fact is now charred and covered be ash. I think the Prosecution has to pick a theory of modality of this crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're not talking about the theory of the crime. We're talking about the door, and I believe it's all fair --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this is burnt, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It is not burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that white ash underneath is not burnt?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's not white ash.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's decay. It could be numerous things, but it's not ash.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. O'Donnell when he saw that picture said it was ash. Did he have the same opportunity to see this as you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe -- I mean, he's not the ash expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would ask for a reference in the transcript to such an admission by Mr. O'Donnell, or was this something that was put to him by close-ended cross-examination by appearance?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to circle the white portion underneath that you say is not burnt wood. Actually, could I ask you to mark it on the ELMO, the hard copy. You'll be provided with a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do we have a transcript reference for Mr. O'Donnell's reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll have to get it for you, the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just for clarification, what do you want me to circle?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The narrow part of the 2 by 4 that's facing downward that it looks white and gray that you say is not burnt; can I ask you to circle that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe he said that the whole thing was not burnt. So that's misleading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Circle the other white and gray part on the this 2 by 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: You want me to circle the part of the 2 by 4 that I think is not touched by flame?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I asked you to circle the white and grey portion of the 2 by 4 which you say in your evidence now is not burnt. That's what I'm asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: None of it's burnt, for the record, but I will circle the grey portion that you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you're certain that that is not burnt?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could look at from the outside, that's 3543, so maybe we -- could that hard copy be put up on the ELMO. And sir, is it your evidence that none of this -- this is the other side of the wedge, is it not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe so, yes. That's the way it appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is not burnt.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
