utterances.text: It is not burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if it were burnt, if it had charring and discolouration from burning, it seems that both ends of the wood have been sawed off, correct, leaving a clean, pristine wooden surface; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It was sawed out at some point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I guess my question to you is, if it's really mold, why would mold only form on the side of it and not on the two ends?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation, lack of foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Restate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You say all the discolouration is mold; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mold knows no difference between the side and the cut edge, does it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if it were mold, we would expect -- if this is the original wedge, sitting here for 17 years gathering mold, wouldn't we expect to see blackening or discolouration on the two sawed ends of this piece of wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. I think we can see some areas --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking for a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just answer the question, and Mr. Alarid, please restrain yourself. The objections do not have any weight if they're of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a mold expert, okay, and just like they're not -- there doesn't appear to be mold on this side, there's mold all through here and all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on. He's not a mold expert. Let's move on, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Will, sir, if it were -- I put to you, sir, that this is a burnt piece of wood from a fire that someone after that fire took it, cut it, and jammed it into in door jam; am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, you are. This is not a burnt piece of wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would tender those exhibits, Your Honour, the hard copies as well as the other copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. McCoy, I have a better picture of the -- where the lock set would be, and I'd ask that you -- we call up Y020-355 -- 3552. That's Y020-3552. Now, sir, we're looking at the portion of the door jam that you wanted to refer to; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, but I would -- I wanted a different angle, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, show us where the indentation -- where the place is for the lock to lock into.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: This angle, I cannot see one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But isn't that the surface of the door jam where we would expect to find that mortice where the bolt would go into?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Somewhere in this area. Is there another angle of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm going to give you all the photos that you took that we can find of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we call up 3553.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps this is this photo that you're speaking about. Now, here's a close-up of it. Mr. McCoy, there's no place to put a bolt in this door jam, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The part that's visible, no. Is there a picture on the back-side of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll look for that, as well, but could I ask you --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... area?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The portion that you've circled, that's the portion that we would expect to find the lock set go into; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Somewhere in here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. And it's not there, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, we'll let the picture speak for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would tender 3553.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 3553 is now an Exhibit P282, and 35 -- the hard copy of the previous exhibit is Exhibit P281, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can we look at Y020-3540. I would ask that the markings be saved as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. McCoy, do you still maintain that there's no possibility that this door was changed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: You're asking me if there's no possibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've drawn the conclusion that it's the original door, and based on that conclusion you've made rather important conclusions about how this fire happened. Are you sure that this is the same door?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The conclusion I came to is this is the same door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you want to reconsider it now?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at Y020-3543. We've seen this before. I'm going to ask that you -- the usher place, again, a printed A3 copy for you and that the Chamber receive a printed copy as well. Now, this picture was taken on the wall outside under the portico of the room that you examined; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it was to the right of the door?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You don't dispute that this shows a serious fire, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: A small fire could have caused that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A small fire.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What would you have to see to make you think that it was a big fire? How would it look different? How would a big fire look different?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Bigger members, wood members being deeper charred. This is lightweight material, and lightweight material, just like paper, burns easily and fairly rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've already explained what alligatoring is, and we can see alligatoring on this; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell by the pattern of alligatoring the intensity of the fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what's your opinion with respect to your observations of the alligatoring in this photo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Areas such as this and this would be deeper, deeper, more defined definition for a more intense, longer-burning fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the deeper the indentation in the alligatoring, the more intense the fire was that caused it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So now based on how deep that is, your assessment is that it's a small fire, it wasn't so deep; is that your assessment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, that is my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd tender that, and I'd ask that it be left up on the screen for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you were to put your finger -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please tender it. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P283, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you were to push your finger into that alligatoring, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: My finger would turn black, and it would -- it would indent it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess what I'm trying to get at is it fragile? Is it very hard? If you pushed against it, would it give way?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It depends on how thick the member is. We use -- in the industry, I have never used it, but we have a depth char-metre, and it's a fine instrument that goes in, and it's not a blunt instrument. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's to measure the depth of the alligatoring?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why did you not use it when you examined this scene?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I've never used it. I'll just saying in our industry. That's not something I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be fair to say that it's softer than the original wood?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's been compromised. I'd say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we were to take this piece and put it in the middle of the floor there and leave it there for 17 years where it would be walked on, it would be rained on, perhaps there would be animals living in it for a year or, so would we still see this kind of alligatoring on it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: How many animals are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's say enough to fill this room.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No. This piece of wood would probably be compromised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would be black, but it would not have the alligatoring on it; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: How long did the animals live there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's say 17 years. It's been walked on on a regular basis, rained on, snowed on. There's not going to be alligatoring like we see here, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, it would be compromised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would still be black, though; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd tender that if I hadn't already. Sorry, I'm losing a bit of track here. I have tendered it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that you now be shown Y020-3538. This is the same area, but it's taking a step back. It's zooming out a little bit. I want to ask you a few questions about that. It's on the screen. Do you confirm that this is a picture of the same area; it's just taken a few steps back, and we can see more of the wall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from this picture we get the sense that at one time this wall was covered with a material; do we not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What leads you to the conclusion that this wall was covered with some finished material?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It looks -- it appears to me that it's lightweight material, and it might have been some type of covering. It also might have been the structure where they poured the actual wall into, a form, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A form? But this wouldn't be strong enough to hold wet concrete, would it, material?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a concrete expert, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if you're not a concrete expert, you're not really able to say it might be the form that they poured concrete into, are you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So how are you able to say that it's a possibility but you're not able to say whether it's strong enough to hold the wet concrete? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I've done it before, but I'm not an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, fire ordinarily burns up and it burns out; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Ordinarily, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is it reasonable to infer from looking at this picture that the material below this was on fire and the fire travelled up to this area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: With the evidence shown that I believe to be true and original, there was no fire below this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So how -- any ideas about what would have happened to the rest of the wall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There's a phenomenon and I told -- it's not really an actual term. It's an actual -- it causes fire. It's drop-down. When the material that you spoke of earlier burnt in whatever year, it possibly dropped down and started this fire. There's rubbish. There's vegetation. I cannot explain how that burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But what I'm just asking for the bare wall immediately under it. Can we not conclude that there was a fire on that portion of the material?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So it's missing now; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it -- it wasn't on the ground underneath this, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I do not recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'd ask you to look at your other pictures. I could not find any material on the ground, but it seems to me if we know there was a finished wall material here, we know that the top portion was burnt, we cannot find the charred remains of the lower portion, to me that seems like pretty clear evidence that someone has cleared it up; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Along with time and years and -- I don't know when this fire happened, sir. I don't know how long ago it happened, and with time everything degrades.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So are you saying that you believe that the lower portion of this wall degraded into the soil underneath?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I don't know where -- I don't know where it's at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you entertain the possibility that perhaps someone cleaned off the finished wall material here and forgot to get this portion up in the corner of the ceiling?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I did not entertain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. This did not indicate to you that someone may have gone back into the scene and tampered with it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, here we see a narrow piece of wood that is commonly referred to as a furring strip in the US and as a batton in many other countries. Do you know the piece that I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe, so but at the same time I don't believe it is what you're saying it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Could I ask you to circle what you believe I'm saying is a furring strip.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that is the piece I'm referring to. You were there. You had a better look than I. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's a portion of the wood as a hole that was not -- it's one piece. It's not two -- you're thinking it's two separate pieces. It's one piece, and this portion was not destroyed by fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you're saying that that thin strip is the same material that we see charred?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's not a piece underneath it on which the top pieces are fixed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No. To my -- to the best of my knowledge no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, explain how that's possible. What's the phenomenon - you're the expert - that we could have two flammable surfaces budding each other and one could be so significantly burnt and one another portion of the very same material is not burnt?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There is some slight discolouration right - I just covered it up - right there, and for whatever reason, the material that was on top, one piece, it's -- in my opinion, this is plywood, plyboard, and it's pressed in layers and glued; and the piece right above it is missing, it's gone, for whatever reason, and this is what was behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So this is a piece of wood behind the plywood on the top.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: No, it's all one. This is not a furring strip that you're referring to. It's all one. You know how plywood is made. They cross grains, and for whatever reason the material that was covering that, protecting that is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now you said you don't know what reason. This is the very purpose of having an expert here. What is the scientific reason that a piece of plywood, a piece of integrated wood, that one portion of it could burn so significantly, and the other portion seemed not to burn remarkably?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, in my expert opinion, I believe there was a piece covering that that did burn completely -- it was uniform. However, the way pressed board is made, it's not there anymore. It's cross -- it's cross-grain. Therefore, the piece on top of that is missing. It's not there. For whatever reason, I don't know .

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So why isn't this piece burnt? That's what I'm driving at.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It was behind it. It's all the same, I wish I could draw you a diagram of how pressboard is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, then. If it's possible that a piece of wood is affixed to -- or is on top of another piece of wood, whether it be the same plywood or something else, it can protect it from fire damage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Depending on the depth or the thickness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But it can do that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's possible in a fire like this that we could peel of the charred lay and are we might find wood underneath that does not look like it's been burnt?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, that does look slightly discoloured. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you don't dispute that there's a remarkable difference between the heavily charred piece and this one that still looks like a piece of wood?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's discoloured. It is discoloured. It's not pristine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your testimony now that this is fire damage, this piece of wood that you've circled?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yeah. The dot in the middle is behind it. I covered it up, but it's discoloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm talking about the part that's not discoloured. The part that still looks like ordinary wood.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, I don't know the shade of wood when it was brand new from the factory. I don't know how discoloured it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll tender that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P284, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could I ask that we call up Y020-3613.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again, I have a large piece -- or a large A3 print of this that hopefully will assist you and the Chamber in understanding your evidence. What we're look at is a piece of board, I believe you said it was embedded in the concrete, and it had no fire damage; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's under the window -- under the window closest to the door; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you saying that this is not a piece of material that was used to affix a finished wall surface on the inside of this room?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation, facts not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, you've drawn significant conclusions from this piece of wood saying it's not burnt.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have an opinion as to whether anything was affixed? I believe you're looking at the wrong one. It should be 3613. What's if number at the top of the one on the ELMO that you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. Let me switch to the ELMO. So is it your opinion that there was something -- do you have an opinion as to whether anything was affixed to this piece of wood?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I've put three yellow tags there with what looks like small nails sticking out of that piece of wood where something may have been attached to it. Do you remember those nails?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Specifically I don't, but it looks like there's one. I don't know about the one on the left or the right, but the one in the -- it appears -- it appears to me that there is one nail in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I would tender that, the hard copy and the electronic copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you actually took a much closer picture. We'll show that next.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P285, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph -- or photograph 11 and 12 of your report, you say: "Window closest to the door with wood beam. Wood beam shows no fire damage." And in photo 2, you say: "Close-up of wood beam beneath window. No signs of smoke or fire damage." Is this your evidence that this is a beam of wood?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's a large diameter -- large as in thick, embedded in the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How are you able to determine that it was large if it's embedded in the concrete?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: The thickness, the length -- I mean, it looks a good three feet, you know, and then it's an inch and a half, two inches thick. That to me is a significant piece of lumber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: And the depth, I don't know. It could go --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's not a furring strip?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: In my opinion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you see -- this is a close-up picture. Do you see the nail where the yellow tag is?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that a nail sticking out indicating that something was affixed to this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's a nail sticking out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's rather low down, so it doesn't seem that it was there to hang a picture, does it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I would guess not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that probability would indicate that someone put a nail into this wood because they were attaching something to this wood?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Attaching what, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, to me it seems also that probability would indicate that they were attaching a finished wall surface. Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is the third time that he's asked a question Your Honour has previously told him to move along with, and I believe Mr. Groome is now testifying as to what is possible to him, which is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's asking the witness whether that's a possibility. What do you say, Witness? Are you able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a furring strip expert. I'm not. That piece of wood is not burnt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Move on now, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, let me just ask one more question about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I mean, you got an A in building. Nails are used to attach --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- things --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Any things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- to wood; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And on this piece of wood, you call it a beam under the window, there are several nails sticking out a small amount from the wood; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I see one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, look down. There's another one to the right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I cannot make that out as a nail. I see one item that possibly looks like a nail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we're having difficulty. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Excuse me, we don't even see the one nail, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to point to the nail that you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is 3613; correct? I'm sorry, 3614.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can you point to it again so the judges can see? You recognise that nail. Now, over to where the yellow tag is, would you remove that yellow tag. Now, point to where -- the area where that was. Just below that, so Their Honours can -- is that not a nail sticking out partially from a piece of wood?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I cannot make out anything there. To me that looks like a nail.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there something sticking out from the wood?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It could be part of this branch. I cannot, with this picture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll move on. Tender it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P286, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we are just a couple minutes away now. How many more questions do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Actually, not too many, Your Honour. I'm not sure that I'll finish today. I will have I think 15, 20 minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can go on, can't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just inquiring whether we can go on until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we okay with the tapes? Who is to provide that answer? Just go on. Just carry on, and let's finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Groome, just try and finish in about ten minutes so that if there is -- are you going to have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. I have probably about four photographs and five, six questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Already. Well, let's take it as far as we can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you be shown Y020-3591. While that's being called up, if I might make use of the time -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you at 5 to 4.00 when we have reached -- so I can do some stock-taking, Mr. Alarid, in relation to the remaining witnesses because we may give you another day, but I want to know before giving you the day that the time will be used profitably.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the piece of wood that we were just talking about that you agree has at least one nail in it is the piece that we can see to the right of this photo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to circle it, please, on the electronic screen.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, now, if I could draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I would tender that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P287, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, on photograph 6 of your report, you say: "Dark areas near left corner are consistent with a small exterior fire." So there was evidence of fire under the portico of the building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your evaluation of the outside, under the portico, there's the fire damage up in the right-hand corner by the ceiling, and there's another area on the left that has fire damage? You talk about dark areas.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay. On photograph 6, my photograph 6 -- do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The problem is, though, the copy we were provided, they were all black. We couldn't really see what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it the same, or is it a different area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's the same area. This picture is facing west, and the area I'm referring to is the same area we just went over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: So at this point, it's to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I understand now. So in your evaluation, you agree that there are at least one fire outside and one and possibly two smaller fires inside; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I believe there was only one fire inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So you --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: And one fire outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So the fire inside is one fire that may have had two causes: Children playing or people keeping warm.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Possibility of either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What made you think that it was children playing or people keeping warm?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There was a large amount of human feces, people possibly hanging out, using this as a shelter, playing, any number of reasons. It's a cold climate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But I guess the thing that strikes me as a little bit curious is, doesn't it seem unusual that someone trying to keep warm would light a fire on the floor that they're sitting on, a wooden floor?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There's portions that are dirt, correct, and I -- I would think that most people would know better than to light a fire on a wood floor just to keep warm, okay, and the area I saw that had small amounts of small-diameter wood was away from the intact wood floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So you're reaching the conclusion that someone lit a fire there to keep warm based on your finding charred wood that was of a small dimension; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, and not just any possibility but possible, probable child's play, kids playing, or keeping warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the wood that you saw burnt, you believe is not the floor but wood that someone brought in to light up and keep themselves warm?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you make that determination?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It was in a small area away from the wood floor and in the diameter. It wasn't wood planks that we saw earlier or that -- that we saw earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, if we took a floor-board, let's say three-quarter inches thick, 6 inches wide, and it was burnt very severely, and then it was placed on the floor, and 17 years of people walking on it, animals walking on it, would it not break up into smaller bits?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, but the amount, it wasn't all over throughout the room. It was just in a smaller area. It was a small, little fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you're drawing that conclusion based on finding some small pieces of burnt wood. Isn't it --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: In a small location. It wasn't throughout the whole room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Isn't it equally consistent that the floor-boards burnt very thoroughly behind the door, the pieces were broken up over time, people walking on it, and someone shovelled out as much as they could, and they missed a few small fragments? Isn't that equally consistent with your theory?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It's not consistent with my theory at all. I mentioned nothing about people shovelling anything out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, how do you know that someone didn't?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I don't know, but the floor-boards that were there, they're still there. The floor is -- the majority of the floor is intact. It's -- in that one corner, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll talk about the floor in a few minutes, perhaps tomorrow morning. Mr. Ivetic has already asked you about that electrical box. I want to ask you to take a look at Y020-3624. If I haven't tendered this, I apologise and would ask to tender it before we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit P288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, what you see on the screen now is something embedded in the wall of the room. Why did you take a picture of these two items embedded in the wall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: I photograph fire scenes thoroughly. If I don't know what it is, I can't explain it, I still photograph it. If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. That's sufficient. When I looked at it, I thought it looked like burnt wood; am I incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: It looks -- it looks dark in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does it look like burnt wood?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Some -- yeah, it could possibly look like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where in the room are these two pieces of burnt wood embedded in the wall?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. Again, misstates the evidence. He has not said that it is burnt wood. That's Mr. Groome testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I stand corrected. Where are these two pieces that look like burnt wood in the room?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Sir, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it inside or is ti outside?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Outside the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it inside the room or in the portico?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Sir, at this time I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you between now and tomorrow morning to please look through all your photographs and be able to answer that question for me tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. So let me move on, then. Now I want to talk about the floor. Before I do that, what is the term accelerant mean in the nomenclature of arson investigation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: An accelerant is an item that is used to accelerate the fire, such as gasoline, some type of ignitable liquid, anything utilised to accelerate or quicken the fire, start up the fire faster, to get it going quicker and faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. You as an investigator, fire investigator, how do you make the determination what signs you look for for whether an accelerant was used?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: There's various ways, and they're all used together. One is obvious, smell, and we also used, which wasn't used on this fire, obviously, a canine, whose smell is much greater -- like, a thousand times greater than ours, and they're trained as accelerant dogs, and they'll clue in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, but you didn't have one of those. What are the other ways?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, like I said, smell, visual signs --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's the part I'm interested in now. What are the visual indications that an accelerant has been used in a fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: An accelerant relating to a liquid, an ignitable liquid would leave circular-type patterns or -- circular-type patterns because liquid flows out, and it's not going to be a sharp, jagged. It's going to be a gradual arc, or circle, possibly even a donut. There's also a donut shaped liquid, little or no burning in the centre but burning around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that when an accelerant is used on a floor, we'll see burning wherever the liquid was; it'll be more significant burning than the rest of the floor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN McCOY
utterances.text: Again, the donut shape with no burning in the centre, there's still ignitable liquid there, but it burns --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why does the gasoline in the middle of the donut --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'm gong to have to stop you now and we'll resume tomorrow morning. Now, let me take stock, Mr. Alarid. How many more witnesses do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have Dr. Linda LaGrange scheduled for tomorrow. We have Officer Benjamin Dimas who is set for -- let's say Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, this is going long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But he's arriving on Saturday, so we were anticipating on starting him Monday. We had -- but, again, if it runs long, we have retired Deputy Chief Cliff Jenkins, who is the police officer investigator, and then we have Dr. Hough, who is the psychologist that -- and then of course, we have seven subpoenas outstanding. We have Vlade Rasic, and technically we have Milan Lukic himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is he going to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: He wants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, so you counted today what? Sounds like four or five?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We have five --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Including those from the subpoenaed witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No. There's seven subpoenas outstanding, three we're hoping to get quick confirmation of receipt and ability to travel, and four would be the ones where we didn't really have any forwarding information for service of process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it looks like you could get three?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning I'll tell you what arrangements will be made. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, did you put in your application for the other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... few applications the Chamber has asked about. You asked us about the experts. I think we filed that. That was due Tuesday. That's been filed. There's rebuttal witnesses ... [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's how many? That's due tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The 20th, as I recall, and that's well underway. And then just so the Chamber is also aware of, we're in the process of finalising an application to open up other portions of the testimony that we believe do not require -- in many cases, it was errors on our part where we just forgot to ask the Chamber to come out of private session, but the Chamber should have that before Friday or Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 8.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
